title: Anterior STEMI / Acute Coronary Syndrome

patient.name: Mike Roberts
patient.complaint: Crushing substernal chest pressure

dispatch: Medic 4, respond lights and sirens to 1420 North Industrial Way, construction site, for a 48-year-old male complaining of severe acute chest pain while unloading materials. Clear and warm conditions.
clues: Heavy 'crushing' substernal chest pressure radiating down left shoulder and arm (OPQRST Q & R)
Hypertensive (160/88 mmHg) and tachycardic (102 bpm) sympathetic drive
Pale, cool, diaphoretic skin with active nausea
Clear bilateral lung sounds (no pulmonary edema)
Prescribed Nitroglycerin on scene; no contraindications (no ED meds, no active bleeding)

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Clear bilaterally in all anterior and posterior fields
baseline_vitals.pupils: PEARRL at 4 mm equal and reactive

reassessment_vitals.pain_score: 4 / 10 ('Feels much lighter, like the heavy weight lifted')

dialogue: Medic 4, respond lights and sirens to commercial construction site for a 48-year-old male experiencing acute chest pain during work.
I understand I am dispatched to a construction site for a 48-year-old male experiencing chest pain during work. BSI precautions on: gloves and eye protection. Is my scene safe?
The nature of illness is non-traumatic acute chest pain. My number of patients is one. Due to the high-acuity nature of illness, I am requesting ALS backup immediately.

I observe a 48-year-old male sitting on a crate, leaning forward, clutching his chest, visibly pale and diaphoretic. I consider C-spine stabilization, but do not suspect trauma, so C-spine is not indicated.
Hello sir, I'm an EMT. What is your name and what did you call 911 for today?
My name is Mike Roberts... man, I'm just having some really serious chest pain right now.
Mr. Roberts is alert, oriented, and speaking in full sentences. His airway is patent. How is my patient's breathing?
Respirations are 24 breaths per minute, slightly shallow and dyspneic.
I am applying high-flow oxygen via non-rebreather mask at 15 liters per minute. Mr. Roberts, do you mind if I touch your wrist to check your pulse?
What is my patient's pulse and skin condition? Do I see any major gross hemorrhage?
Radial pulse is 102 bpm, regular and strong. Skin is pale, cool, and diaphoretic. No gross bleeding.

I have determined this to be a high-priority, load-and-go patient due to suspected acute coronary syndrome. Partner, please obtain a full set of baseline vitals while I begin OPQRST and SAMPLE history with Mr. Roberts.
Mr. Roberts, what were you doing today when all of this started?
I was helping unload a bunch of heavy steel pipe out there on the yard.
Does anything make the pain better or worse, like resting or moving around?
Seems like moving around makes it worse, but resting here hasn't stopped it.
Can you describe the pain to me in your own words?
It really feels like someone parked a forklift on my chest... heavy, crushing pressure.
Can you show me where it hurts, and does that pain go anywhere else?
Right here in the center of my chest, and it shoots straight down my left arm and into my shoulder.
On a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the worst pain you've ever felt, where is it right now?
It's an 8 out of 10. Easily an 8.
About how long ago did this start?
Are you having any other symptoms today, like dizziness, shortness of breath, or nausea?
A little short of breath, and right now I feel pretty nauseous, like I might throw up.
Do you have any allergies to medications?
I'm allergic to penicillin. That's it.
What medications do you take, and have you taken any today?
I've got this Nitro prescription in my pocket. I took one pill about 5 minutes before you got here.
Did that Nitro pill help the pain at all?
Took the edge off just a tiny bit, but it's still pounding at an 8.
Do you have a history of heart problems or why you take Nitro?
Yeah, I had a heart attack two years ago, and my doctor gave me the pills for angina.
When was the last thing you had to eat or drink?
I drank a bottle of cold water about 10 minutes ago.
Did anything unusual happen before this started, other than unloading pipe?
No, just a regular workday until my chest exploded.
Mr. Roberts, I'm going to listen to your lungs on your back, then check your chest. Lean forward for me and take deep breaths. What are my lung sounds?
Breath sounds are clear and equal bilaterally in all lung bases and apices.
I auscultate heart tones and palpate your chest wall. Does it hurt more when I push on your ribs?
No, pushing on it doesn't change it. The pain is deep inside.
Partner, what are the baseline vitals?
BP is 160/88 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 24, SpO2 97% on NRB, BGL 101 mg/dL, pupils PEARRL at 4 mm.
Mr. Roberts, do you have any stomach ulcers, active bleeding, recent stroke, or asthma?
Have you taken any erectile dysfunction medications such as Viagra, Cialis, or Levitra within the past 48 hours?
I am administering 324 mg of chewable baby aspirin (four 81 mg tablets). Mr. Roberts, please chew these completely before swallowing.

I inspect Mr. Roberts's nitroglycerin: right patient, right medication 0.4 mg sublingual tablet, expiration date is next year, tablets are clear and dry. Systolic BP is 160 mmHg (>100 mmHg). I contact Medical Control.

Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. I am on scene with a 48-year-old male with suspected acute myocardial infarction. Vitals: BP 160/88, HR 102, lungs clear. No contraindications or ED meds. Patient took one prescribed Nitro 5 minutes ago with minimal relief. I request authorization to assist with a second dose of 0.4 mg sublingual nitroglycerin.
Medic 4, this is Medical Control. You are authorized to assist with one 0.4 mg sublingual nitroglycerin tablet. Recheck BP in 5 minutes.
Medical Control, I copy and confirm: I am authorized to assist with one 0.4 mg sublingual nitroglycerin tablet and recheck BP in 5 minutes. Candidate out.
Mr. Roberts, place this tablet under your tongue and let it dissolve. It may cause a tingling sensation, a throbbing headache, or mild lightheadedness as it opens up your coronary arteries.
I package the patient and begin transport. I reassess my patient every 5 minutes: level of consciousness, breathing effort, pain score, and repeat vitals. What are my 5-minute findings?
Mr. Roberts states chest pain has decreased to a 4 out of 10. Repeat vitals: BP 134/76 mmHg, HR 94 bpm, RR 18 breaths/min, SpO2 99% on NRB.

I provide verbal hand-off report to the incoming ALS paramedic crew: 'This is Mike Roberts, a 48-year-old male presenting with acute substernal crushing chest pain radiating to his left arm, onset 35 minutes ago while unloading heavy materials. Initially rated 8/10 with shortness of breath, diaphoresis, and nausea. History of MI and angina; allergic to penicillin. Baseline vitals: BP 160/88, HR 102, RR 24, SpO2 97%, BGL 101, lungs clear bilaterally. We placed him on 15 L NRB, administered 324 mg chewable aspirin, and assisted with one 0.4 mg sublingual Nitro under medical direction. Repeat vitals: BP 134/76, HR 94, RR 18, and pain has dropped to 4/10. He is stable and ready for your 12-lead.'
Are there any questions? Is there anything else you would like to do?
No questions, and there is nothing else I would like to do. I am done with this station.
hand_off_report: Mike Roberts, 48M, acute crushing substernal chest pain radiating down left arm, onset 35 mins ago during exertion. Baseline BP 160/88, HR 102, lungs clear bilaterally. History of angina/MI; allergic to penicillin. Administered 15L NRB, 324 mg chewable aspirin, and 0.4 mg sublingual Nitro per medical control. Repeat vitals BP 134/76, HR 94, RR 18, pain reduced from 8/10 to 4/10. Ready for 12-lead transfer.
critical_traps: Failure to verbalize BSI precautions and scene safety prior to touching patient.
Failure to recognize acute coronary syndrome as an immediate high-priority load-and-go emergency.
Administering nitroglycerin without explicitly screening for phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (Viagra/Cialis within 24-48 hrs).
Administering nitroglycerin without checking systolic BP (must be >100 mmHg).
Failing to perform closed-loop verbatim repeat-back of Medical Control physician orders.

differential_matrix.clue: Pain reproducible with direct chest palpation / movement
differential_matrix.impact: Nitroglycerin and aspirin contraindicated; non-ischemic etiology.

differential_matrix.clue: Maximal sudden tearing pain between shoulder blades, BP discrepancy >20 mmHg between arms
differential_matrix.impact: Aspirin is lethal; patient requires immediate vascular surgery.

differential_matrix.clue: Burning epigastric pain provoked by lying flat, relieved by antacids
differential_matrix.impact: Always treat as ACS until ruled out by serial troponins and 12-lead ECG.

title: Acute Inferior-RV STEMI (The Nitroglycerin Preload Trap)

patient.name: Arthur Miller
patient.complaint: Severe epigastric burning, nausea, extreme weakness

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 to 842 Elmwood Drive for a 62-year-old male with severe weakness, indigestion, and profound nausea. Caller sounds sluggish.
clues: Epigastric burning discomfort often mistaken for heartburn/indigestion
Severe sinus bradycardia (HR 48 bpm) from right coronary artery (RCA) ischemia feeding the AV node
Borderline systolic blood pressure (BP 108/64 mmHg)
Profuse cold diaphoresis and gray/ashen skin
LETHAL TRAP: Nitroglycerin causes catastrophic venodilation, destroying preload in right ventricular infarcts and triggering profound shock/cardiac arrest

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Clear bilaterally in all bases (lungs are dry because right side isn't pumping blood forward)

reassessment_vitals.pain_score: 7 / 10 (unchanged, but hemodynamically stable without preload crash)

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 response to 842 Elmwood Drive, 62-year-old male with severe weakness, indigestion, and nausea.
Dispatched to residential address for 62M with severe weakness and indigestion. BSI precautions: gloves, eye protection. Scene safe?
Nature of illness: suspected acute cardiac event. One patient. I am dispatching ALS backup immediately due to cardiac suspicion.
General impression: 62-year-old male slumped in recliner, gray/ashen complexion, profuse forehead diaphoresis. No trauma noted, C-spine not indicated.
Hello sir, my name is EMT Luke. What is going on today?
I just feel... terribly weak. My stomach is on fire... thought it was indigestion from lunch, but I'm cold and sick.
Patient is alert to verbal, oriented x 4, speaking in sentences. Airway is patent. How is breathing?
SpO2 is 93%. I place the patient on 4 L/min oxygen via nasal cannula to titrate between 94-98%. Checking pulse and skin.
Radial pulse is 48 beats per minute, weak and bradycardic. Skin is cold, ashen, and drenched in sweat. No bleeding.

This is an immediate high-priority load-and-go patient. The combination of bradycardia, diaphoresis, and epigastric pain indicates acute inferior wall MI. Partner, obtain baseline vitals immediately while I complete history.
Arthur, when did this burning pain in your upper stomach start?
About an hour ago while sitting watching TV. Came on out of nowhere.
Does anything make it better or worse? Did you try Tums or antacids?
Took three Tums 30 minutes ago... did nothing at all.
Can you describe what it feels like?
Heavy gnawing ache right under my ribs. Like a hot rock pressing down.
Does it move into your jaw, neck, back, or arms?
A little bit into my lower jaw and my neck feels tight.
On a 1 to 10 scale, 10 being the worst, how bad is it?
It's a solid 7. I feel like I'm gonna pass out.
Metformin for diabetes, lisinopril for blood pressure. My wife has Nitro in the cabinet.
Have you taken any Viagra, Cialis, or Levitra recently?
Partner, what are the baseline vitals?
BP is 108/64 mmHg, HR 48 bpm, RR 20, SpO2 93% on room air, BGL 114 mg/dL, pupils PEARRL 3 mm, lung sounds clear bilaterally.
I auscultate Arthur's lungs: clear in all fields. I palpate the abdomen: soft, non-tender, non-distended. Pain is not abdominal wall muscular.
I am administering 324 mg of chewable baby aspirin (four 81 mg tablets) immediately, instructing Arthur to chew completely. Aspirin prevents platelet aggregation.

CRITICAL CLINICAL DECISION: I WILL NOT ADMINISTER OR ASSIST WITH NITROGLYCERIN. With a heart rate of 48 bpm and a borderline BP of 108/64 in an inferior MI presentation, right ventricular involvement is highly suspected. Right ventricular infarctions depend entirely on venous preload; nitroglycerin venodilation will crash his blood pressure and induce cardiogenic shock.

I contact Medical Control: 'Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. On scene with a 62-year-old male presenting with suspected inferior STEMI: epigastric burning radiating to jaw, diaphoresis, BP 108/64, HR 48 sinus bradycardia, lungs clear. 324 mg chewable aspirin administered. Due to profound bradycardia and high risk of RV preload collapse, I am withholding nitroglycerin and initiating rapid transport with ALS rendezvous.'
Medic 4, excellent clinical judgment. Do NOT administer nitroglycerin. Maintain supine position, keep warm, and meet ALS at station 42.
Medical Control, confirmed: Withholding nitroglycerin, transporting supine to intercept Medic 1 ALS at station 42. Candidate out.
We package Arthur supine on the cot to maximize venous return, apply warm blankets, and begin transport. 5-minute reassessment:
Arthur remains alert. Pain remains 7/10. Repeat vitals: BP 106/62 mmHg, HR 50 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 98% on 4 L NC.

Verbal Hand-Off to ALS Paramedics: 'This is Arthur Miller, 62M, presenting with suspected inferior wall STEMI. 1-hour history of severe epigastric burning radiating to lower jaw with cold diaphoresis and presyncope. No relief from antacids. No drug allergies. Baseline vitals: BP 108/64, HR 48 bpm, RR 20, SpO2 93%, BGL 114 mg/dL, lungs completely clear. We placed him on 4 L NC (SpO2 now 98%) and administered 324 mg chewable aspirin. Nitroglycerin was deliberately withheld due to bradycardia (HR 48) and borderline BP to prevent RV preload collapse. Current BP 106/62, HR 50. He is prepped for immediate 12-lead right-sided V4R view.'
hand_off_report: Arthur Miller, 62M, suspected acute inferior-RV STEMI presenting with severe epigastric burning radiating to the jaw, profound weakness, and diaphoresis. Baseline BP 108/64, HR 48 bpm (sinus bradycardia), lungs clear bilaterally. Administered 4L NC and 324 mg chewable aspirin. Nitroglycerin was deliberately withheld to protect preload against right ventricular infarction. Repeat BP 106/62, HR 50, SpO2 98%. Prepped for right-sided V4R 12-lead ECG.
critical_traps: Giving Nitroglycerin to a bradycardic (HR < 50 bpm) or borderline hypotensive patient (Automatic Critical Fail!).
Dismissing epigastric burning as simple GERD or food poisoning without performing cardiac evaluation in a geriatric/diabetic patient.
Failing to administer 324 mg chewable aspirin in suspected acute coronary syndrome.
Sitting the patient upright during right ventricular failure (worsens venous return; keep supine/semi-Fowler's).

differential_matrix.clue: Tachycardia (HR > 100), hypertension, crushing retrosternal pain
differential_matrix.impact: Nitroglycerin is safe and indicated; reduces LV afterload.

differential_matrix.clue: Focal epigastric tenderness on deep palpation, normal HR, warm dry skin
differential_matrix.impact: Non-ischemic, but requires 12-lead rule-out in elderly patients.

differential_matrix.clue: Right upper quadrant pain provoked by fatty meals, Murphy's sign positive, fever
differential_matrix.impact: Surgical abdomen; no cardiac ischemia.

title: Acute Left-Sided Congestive Heart Failure / Flash Pulmonary Edema

patient.name: Evelyn Hayes
patient.complaint: Severe suffocating shortness of breath, pink frothy sputum

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to 312 Willow Creek Lane for a 71-year-old female in acute severe respiratory distress. Caller states patient cannot catch her breath and is coughing up pink liquid.
clues: Profound orthopnea (cannot lie flat) and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (woke up gasping)
Productive cough with classic pink, frothy sputum (capillary transudate in alveoli)
Diffuse bilateral wet inspiratory crackles (rales) extending from lung bases to mid-zones ('cardiac asthma')
Severe hypertensive crisis (BP 198/110 mmHg) driving fluid across the alveolar-capillary membrane

LETHAL TRAP: Auscultating wheezing and misdiagnosing as COPD/Asthma to give Albuterol (Albuterol tachycardia causes fatal myocardial oxygen demand in CHF); treatment of choice is High-PEEP CPAP + Nitroglycerin

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Diffuse wet coarse crackles/rales in all posterior lower and middle lung fields bilaterally, scattered cardiac wheezes

reassessment_vitals.lung_sounds: Crackles diminished to basilar zones only
reassessment_vitals.pain_score: 4 / 10 ('I can finally pull air into my chest')

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 response to 312 Willow Creek Lane, 71-year-old female in acute respiratory distress coughing up pink fluid.
Dispatched to 71F with severe respiratory distress and pink sputum. BSI precautions: gloves, eye protection, N-95 mask. Is my scene safe?
Nature of illness: severe acute respiratory compromise / suspected pulmonary edema. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately.
General impression: 71-year-old female sitting bolt upright in armchair, tripod position, gasping for air, cyanotic lips, coughing frothy secretions into tissues. No trauma, C-spine not indicated.
Hello ma'am, I'm EMT Luke. We are here to help you. Can you tell me your name?
Evelyn... (gasp)... can't... breathe... feels like... drowning...
Airway is patent but bubbling with thin secretions. Suction is on standby. Breathing is 32 breaths/min, severely labored with retractions.
SpO2 is 86%. This patient is in impending respiratory failure from flash pulmonary edema. I assemble the CPAP circuit immediately.
Checking circulation: radial pulse is 116 bpm rapid and bounding. Skin is pale, cool, clammy, and peripherally cyanotic. Bilateral pitting pedal edema noted at ankles.
High priority load-and-go. Partner, get baseline vitals immediately while I coach Evelyn onto CPAP and begin SAMPLE history.
Evelyn, this mask is going to blow gentle continuous air pressure to push the water out of your lungs. Hold it against your face while I secure the straps. Breathe slow and deep.
CPAP is applied at 8 cmH2O with 100% oxygen. Evelyn is tolerating the mask.
Evelyn, did this start suddenly while sleeping?
(Nods vigorously behind mask)... woke up at 2 AM... gasping... couldn't lie flat.
How many pillows do you normally sleep on?
Usually... three pillows... tonight even sitting... suffocating.
Do you have any chest pain right now, or just the drowning feeling?
Chest feels tight... heavy... no sharp pain.
Partner, what are the baseline vitals?
BP is 198/110 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, RR 32, SpO2 86% rising to 91% on CPAP, BGL 138 mg/dL, pupils PEARRL 3 mm.
I auscultate lung sounds: diffuse coarse wet crackles/rales in bilateral lower and middle lung fields with scattered cardiac expiratory wheezing.

CLINICAL WARNING & TRAP: Although expiratory wheezing is present, this is 'cardiac asthma' caused by peribronchial interstitial edema. I WILL NOT ADMINISTER ALBUTEROL. Albuterol beta-1 stimulation would increase heart rate, elevate myocardial oxygen demand, and worsen left ventricular failure.
Evelyn, are you allergic to any medications?
Lasix... water pill... lisinopril... metoprolol... and Nitro tablets.
Did you miss your Lasix water pill today or eat a salty meal?
Missed Lasix... two days... ran out.
Have you taken any erectile dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension meds (Revatio/Adcirca)?
Evelyn's systolic BP is 198 mmHg. In severe pulmonary edema with hypertension, nitroglycerin sublingual reduces venous preload and systemic afterload. I contact Medical Control.

Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. On scene with a 71-year-old female in acute pulmonary edema from CHF exacerbation. BP is 198/110, HR 116, SpO2 91% on CPAP @ 8 cmH2O. Bilateral crackles. No ED medications. Requesting authorization to assist with patient's prescribed sublingual nitroglycerin 0.4 mg while maintaining CPAP.
Medic 4, authorized: briefly break mask seal to administer 0.4 mg sublingual nitroglycerin, reseal CPAP, and monitor BP every 5 minutes.
Medical Control, copy and confirm: Authorized for 0.4 mg sublingual nitroglycerin under CPAP seal with 5-minute BP monitoring. Candidate out.
I administer one 0.4 mg sublingual nitroglycerin tablet, reseal the CPAP mask firmly, and keep Evelyn seated fully upright at 90 degrees.
Evelyn is breathing easier. Crackles have receded to lung bases. Repeat vitals: BP 164/92 mmHg, HR 98 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 94% on CPAP.

Verbal Hand-Off Report to ALS Paramedics: 'This is Evelyn Hayes, 71F, presenting with acute left-sided heart failure and flash pulmonary edema. Woke up at 0200 with severe orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and pink frothy sputum after missing Lasix for 2 days. Baseline vitals: BP 198/110, HR 116, RR 32, SpO2 86% on room air with diffuse bilateral crackles and pitting ankle edema. We placed her on CPAP at 8 cmH2O with 100% O2, kept her seated upright at 90 degrees, and administered one 0.4 mg sublingual Nitro under medical direction. Repeat vitals: BP 164/92, HR 98, RR 22, SpO2 94% on CPAP. Crackles are now localized to bases only and she is stable for hospital transfer.'
hand_off_report: Evelyn Hayes, 71F, acute decompensated heart failure / flash pulmonary edema secondary to missed diuretic doses. Presenting with severe orthopnea, pink frothy sputum, and bilateral crackles. Baseline BP 198/110, HR 116, RR 32, SpO2 86%. Initiated CPAP @ 8 cmH2O, kept upright at 90 degrees, administered 0.4 mg sublingual Nitro per medical control. Repeat vitals BP 164/92, HR 98, RR 22, SpO2 94%. Secretions controlled and distress significantly relieved.
critical_traps: Laying a patient with pulmonary edema flat (drowns the patient in their own alveolar fluid).
Administering Albuterol for wheezing in CHF (cardiac asthma trap: beta-1 stimulation can trigger fatal ventricular arrhythmias or MI).
Failing to initiate CPAP or high-flow positive pressure ventilation when SpO2 < 90% in flash pulmonary edema.
Administering Nitroglycerin if systolic BP drops below 100 mmHg.

differential_matrix.clue: Chronic smoker, barrel chest, rhonchi/wheezing without wet rales, normal/low BP, no pink sputum
differential_matrix.impact: Albuterol/Atrovent indicated; low-dose O2 titration.

differential_matrix.clue: High fever, chills, purulent yellow/green sputum, localized rhonchi or consolidation
differential_matrix.impact: Antibiotics indicated; CPAP with caution; no nitroglycerin.

differential_matrix.clue: Sudden onset dyspnea with clear lung sounds, normal chest X-ray appearance, refractory hypoxia
differential_matrix.impact: No pulmonary edema fluid; CPAP does not resolve shunt.

title: Cardiogenic Shock Secondary to Massive Myocardial Infarction

patient.name: Harold Vance
patient.complaint: Profound lethargy, fainting, cold mottled skin, severe hypotension

dispatch: Medic 4, respond code 3 to Westside Medical Clinic, 500 Park Avenue, for a 67-year-old male who collapsed in the waiting room. Clinic staff reporting unrecordable blood pressure and weak thready pulse.
clues: Profound hypotension (BP 82/54 mmHg) caused by massive left ventricular pump failure (>40% myocardial necrosis)
Tachycardic, weak, thready, irregular pulse (HR 118 bpm) attempting to compensate for collapsed stroke volume
Cold, pale, clammy, mottled skin with delayed capillary refill (>4 seconds)
Altered mental status / somnolence from cerebral hypoperfusion
LETHAL TRAP: Nitroglycerin is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED (systolic BP < 100); patient requires immediate supine positioning, high-flow O2, and ALS vasopressor (Dopamine/Norepinephrine) support

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Bilateral basilar crackles (pulmonary vascular congestion)
baseline_vitals.pain_score: 5 / 10 dull crushing chest ache, masked by somnolence

dialogue: Medic 4, code 3 to Westside Medical Clinic, 67-year-old male collapsed in waiting room, hypotensive.
Dispatched to medical clinic for 67M in shock. BSI precautions on: gloves, goggles. Is the scene safe?
Scene is safe. Clinic staff is present.
Nature of illness: cardiogenic shock / cardiac collapse. One patient. Requesting ALS intercept immediately.
General impression: 67-year-old male slumped in clinic chair, ashen gray, lips cyanotic, profoundly lethargic. No trauma, C-spine not indicated.
Sir, can you hear me? Open your eyes.
(Groans softly, eyes flicker open)... so cold... chest hurts...
Airway is patent, no snoring or gurgling. Respirations are 28 breaths/min, shallow. SpO2 is 88%. I place high-flow O2 via Non-Rebreather at 15 L/min.
Checking circulation: radial pulse is barely palpable, rapid and thready at 118 bpm. Skin is ice cold, clammy, and mottled across knees. Cap refill 4 seconds.
IMMEDIATE CRITICAL LOAD-AND-GO. The patient is in decompensated cardiogenic shock. We must move him supine to the stretcher immediately to support cerebral perfusion.
Partner, get baseline vitals immediately while I obtain history from clinic staff and the patient's chart.
He arrived complaining of 2 hours of heavy chest pressure. While waiting, he turned gray and collapsed. His baseline BP here was 82/54 mmHg.
Baseline vitals confirmed: BP 82/54, HR 118 weak, RR 28, SpO2 88% rising to 96% on NRB, BGL 92 mg/dL. Lung sounds reveal wet crackles in both bases.
CLINICAL CONTRAINDICATION: NITROGLYCERIN IS ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED. Systolic BP is 82 mmHg (<100 mmHg). Administering a vasodilator would induce complete cardiovascular collapse.
Can Harold swallow aspirin? Harold, can you chew four small tablets for me?
Administering 324 mg chewable baby aspirin with close airway monitoring. Patient is covered with warm blankets to conserve core body heat.

Contacting Medical Control: 'Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. On scene with a 67-year-old male in decompensated cardiogenic shock secondary to acute MI. BP 82/54, HR 118 thready, RR 28, SpO2 96% on 15L NRB. Lung sounds reveal basilar crackles. 324 mg aspirin given, Nitro strictly withheld. Patient is supine and warm. Requesting expedited ALS intercept for IV fluid titration and vasopressor/dopamine push.'
Medic 4, orders understood. Maintain supine posture, high-flow O2, and expedite transport to meet ALS Medic 2 en route.
Medical Control, confirmed: Supine positioning, high-flow O2, rapid transport to intercept Medic 2. Candidate out.
Patient remains lethargic but responds to voice. BP 84/56 mmHg, HR 114 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 96% on NRB.

ALS Verbal Hand-Off Report: 'This is Harold Vance, 67M, presenting in decompensated cardiogenic shock secondary to acute massive myocardial infarction. 2-hour onset of heavy chest pressure culminating in syncope. Baseline vitals: BP 82/54, HR 118 thready and irregular, RR 28, SpO2 88%, skin cold, clammy, and mottled with delayed cap refill of 4 seconds. Wet crackles in lung bases. We placed him on 15L NRB, positioned him supine, kept him warm, and administered 324 mg chewable aspirin. Nitroglycerin was strictly withheld due to hypotension. Repeat BP is 84/56, HR 114. He requires immediate central venous access, cautious fluid challenge, and vasopressor infusion.'
hand_off_report: Harold Vance, 67M, decompensated cardiogenic shock following massive acute MI. Presenting with syncope, lethargy, cold mottled skin, delayed cap refill, and basilar crackles. Baseline BP 82/54, HR 118 thready, RR 28, SpO2 88%. Interventions: 15L NRB, supine positioning, thermal protection, 324 mg chewable aspirin; nitroglycerin strictly avoided. Repeat BP 84/56, HR 114, SpO2 96%. Immediate ALS vasopressor and cath lab activation required.
critical_traps: Administering nitroglycerin to a patient with systolic BP < 100 mmHg (fatal drop in coronary perfusion).
Failing to recognize cardiogenic shock and sitting the patient upright (deprives brain of critical blood flow).
Failing to warm a patient in shock (hypothermia impairs coagulation and cardiac enzyme kinetics).
Delaying transport on scene rather than executing an immediate load-and-go.

differential_matrix.clue: High fever, warm flushed skin early ('warm shock'), source of infection (UTI/pneumonia)
differential_matrix.impact: Aggressive crystalloid fluid boluses indicated; non-cardiac etiology.

differential_matrix.clue: Clear lung sounds, history of trauma or GI bleed, flat neck veins
differential_matrix.impact: Fluid resuscitation indicated; no pulmonary congestion.

differential_matrix.clue: Hives, facial angioedema, wheezing/stridor, acute allergen exposure
differential_matrix.impact: IM Epinephrine is first-line drug of choice.

title: Acute Thoracic Aortic Dissection (The Tearing Pain Trap)

patient.name: Frank Castillo
patient.complaint: Sudden excruciating ripping pain between shoulder blades

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to 1944 Oak Ridge Court for a 59-year-old male with sudden onset of unbearable back and chest pain. Patient is crying out in agony.
clues: Maximal pain intensity from the exact moment of onset (no gradual buildup)
Excruciating 'tearing', 'ripping', or 'knife-like' sensation radiating straight through to the interscapular back
Significant blood pressure discrepancy (>20 mmHg) between the right and left arms
Unequal or absent peripheral pulses (radial or femoral pulse deficit)
LETHAL TRAP: Misdiagnosing as STEMI and administering ASPIRIN. Aspirin irreversibly impairs platelet function and accelerates fatal aortic rupture and cardiac tamponade!

baseline_vitals.bp: Right arm: 184/102 mmHg | Left arm: 142/80 mmHg (>40 mmHg discrepancy!)
baseline_vitals.hr: 108 bpm (bounding right radial, weak left radial)
baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Clear bilaterally
baseline_vitals.pain_score: 10 / 10 ('The worst pain of my entire life, like I am being torn in half')

reassessment_vitals.bp: Right arm: 178/98 mmHg | Left arm: 138/76 mmHg

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 to 1944 Oak Ridge Court, 59-year-old male with sudden unbearable tearing back and chest pain.
Dispatched to 59M with severe tearing back pain. BSI: gloves, eye protection. Is the scene safe?
Nature of illness: suspected acute vascular catastrophe / aortic dissection. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately.
General impression: 59-year-old male hunched forward on workbench stool, clutching his back and chest, grimacing in agony, diaphoretic. No trauma, C-spine not indicated.
Sir, I'm an EMT. What is your name?

Vitals obtained: Right arm BP is 184/102 mmHg. Left arm BP is 142/80 mmHg. Pulse 108, RR 26, SpO2 95% on room air, BGL 118 mg/dL, lungs clear bilaterally.

patient.name: Maya Lin
patient.complaint: Severe suffocating wheezing, silent chest impending arrest

Monosyllabic or 1-word dyspnea (nodding only, cannot form phrases)
High-pitched inspiratory and expiratory wheezes rapidly diminishing to a 'SILENT CHEST' (loss of wheezing signals near-fatal complete airway closure, not improvement!)

CRITICAL PROTOCOL: Continuous Albuterol (2.5 mg) / Ipratropium (0.5 mg) nebulizer combined with immediate Intramuscular Epinephrine (0.3 mg 1:1,000) for severe bronchospasm with impending respiratory failure

reassessment_vitals.lung_sounds: Prominent, loud expiratory wheezing restored throughout all fields (indicates air movement restored!)
reassessment_vitals.pain_score: 4 / 10 ('My chest opened up, I can draw air in')

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 to Campus Library 3rd floor, 22-year-old female having severe asthma attack, unable to breathe.
Dispatched to 22F with severe asthma. BSI: gloves, eye protection. Scene safe?
Scene is safe. Bystanders are anxious.
Nature of illness: severe acute asthma / status asthmaticus. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately due to impending respiratory arrest.
General impression: 22-year-old female in rigid tripod position with hands braced on knees, profound retractions, pale with circumoral cyanosis. No trauma, C-spine not indicated.
Hello, I'm EMT Luke. Don't try to speak. Nod if you can hear me.
(Nods frantically, gasping for air, unable to speak a single word).
Airway is patent but severely restricted. Respirations are 34 breaths/min, extremely shallow, prolonged exhalation. SpO2 is 87%. I immediately assemble an Albuterol/Atrovent SVN nebulizer.
Checking circulation: radial pulse is 130 bpm, rapid and regular. Skin is pale, cool, and diaphoretic. Cap refill is 3 seconds. High-priority load-and-go.
Partner, obtain baseline vitals immediately and prep the stretcher while I initiate emergency nebulizer therapy.
I auscultate Maya's lungs: What are my lung sounds?
Breath sounds are severely diminished bilaterally with almost no air movement. Faint expiratory wheezes in upper fields, lower fields are nearly silent.

CRITICAL CLINICAL ALERT: A silent chest in severe asthma represents impending asphyxiation and respiratory arrest from complete airway narrowing. I assemble an SVN nebulizer with Albuterol 2.5 mg and Ipratropium Bromide (Atrovent) 0.5 mg, hooked to 6-8 L/min O2.

Maya has her prescribed Albuterol inhaler in hand, completely empty after taking 10 puffs before arrival. With silent chest and exhaustion, aerosolized meds alone may not penetrate the terminal bronchioles. I prepare for Intramuscular Epinephrine administration.
Vitals: BP 136/84 mmHg, HR 130, RR 34, SpO2 87% on room air, BGL 106 mg/dL, pupils PEARRL 4 mm.

I contact Medical Control: 'Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. On scene with a 22-year-old female in status asthmaticus with silent chest and severe exhaustion. SpO2 is 87%, HR 130, RR 34. Continuous Albuterol/Atrovent nebulizer initiated. Due to impending respiratory failure, I request authorization to administer Epinephrine 1:1,000 (1 mg/mL) 0.3 mg intramuscularly into the lateral thigh.'
Medic 4, this is Medical Control. Authorization GRANTED for Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM into the anterolateral thigh. Continue nebulizer and expedite transport.
Medical Control, I copy and confirm: Authorized for Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM into the anterolateral thigh, continue continuous nebulizer, expedite transport. Candidate out.

I verify the 6 Rights of Epinephrine: Right patient, Right medication (Epinephrine 1:1,000 / 1 mg/mL), Right dose (0.3 mg = 0.3 mL), Right route (IM), Right time, Right documentation. Clear fluid, in date. I cleanse the lateral thigh with alcohol and inject at 90 degrees, holding for 10 seconds.
We place Maya seated upright on the stretcher, maintain nebulizer mist, and initiate rapid transport.
Maya's breathing is deeper. Auscultation reveals loud, bilateral expiratory wheezes throughout all lobes. Repeat vitals: BP 142/86 mmHg, HR 124 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 95% on nebulizer.

CLINICAL INTERPRETATION: Hearing loud wheezes now is a POSITIVE sign. It confirms that the beta-2 bronchodilation from IM Epinephrine and Albuterol opened the collapsed bronchioles, restoring vital air exchange.

ALS Verbal Hand-Off Report: 'This is Maya Lin, 22F, presenting with status asthmaticus and silent chest impending respiratory arrest. Emptied her inhaler prior to arrival with no relief. Baseline vitals: BP 136/84, HR 130, RR 34, SpO2 87% on room air with severe accessory muscle use and virtually absent breath sounds. We initiated continuous Albuterol 2.5 mg / Atrovent 0.5 mg nebulizer and administered Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM (1:1,000) under medical control authorization. Repeat vitals: BP 142/86, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 95%. Air movement is restored with bilateral loud expiratory wheezing. She is prepped for ongoing nebulizers and ALS magnesium sulfate/steroids.'
hand_off_report: Maya Lin, 22F, status asthmaticus presenting with silent chest, accessory muscle exhaustion, and 1-word dyspnea. Baseline BP 136/84, HR 130, RR 34, SpO2 87%. Administered continuous Albuterol (2.5 mg) / Atrovent (0.5 mg) nebulizer and 0.3 mg Epinephrine IM (1:1,000) under online medical direction. Repeat vitals BP 142/86, HR 124, RR 22, SpO2 95% with restored loud expiratory air exchange. Transporting upright.

Failing to administer IM Epinephrine when status asthmaticus is failing inhaled bronchodilators.
Laying an asthmatic patient supine (causes immediate suffocation).
Failing to titrate or run nebulizers at adequate flow rates (must run at 6-8 L/min O2).

Assisting with patient's prescribed Albuterol/Combivent MDI using a spacer

baseline_vitals.spo2: 84% on room air (daughter states his normal baseline is 88-90%)
baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Distant breath sounds bilaterally with coarse rhonchi in upper fields and end-expiratory wheezing

reassessment_vitals.lung_sounds: Rhonchi clearing with productive cough, wheezing softened

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 2 response to 514 Sycamore Street, 68-year-old male with COPD exacerbation.
Dispatched to 68M with COPD exacerbation. BSI precautions: gloves, eye protection, N95 mask. Is the scene safe?
Nature of illness: acute respiratory compromise / COPD exacerbation. One patient. Requesting ALS backup due to respiratory distress in a compromised pulmonary patient.

Hello Mr. Miller, I'm EMT Luke. How are you feeling right now?
Tight... real tight in the chest... been getting worse... since Tuesday.
Airway is patent. Respirations are 26 breaths/min with active pursed-lip breathing and prolonged exhalation. SpO2 is 84% on room air.

TARGETED OXYGENATION PROTOCOL: For a known COPD patient, standard protocol targets SpO2 between 88% and 92% to avoid blunting hypoxic drive while preventing tissue hypoxia. I apply oxygen via nasal cannula at 3 L/min.
Checking circulation: radial pulse is 104 bpm, regular. Skin is warm, pink, and dry. Cap refill is 2.5 seconds. No gross bleeding. Priority load-and-go.
Partner, please obtain full baseline vitals while I conduct OPQRST and review George's medications.
George, did this shortness of breath start suddenly, or has it built up over days?
Built up over three days... started with a chest cold... coughing up thick yellowish mucus.
Pursed-lip breathing helps keep my airways from collapsing, and my inhaler helped yesterday, but not today.
Do you have any chest pain?
No sharp pain, just tired muscles from working so hard to breathe.
Are you allergic to any medications?
Spiriva once daily, and this ProAir Albuterol inhaler for flare-ups. I also have 2 liters of home oxygen at night.
Baseline vitals: BP 148/88 mmHg, HR 104 bpm, RR 26, SpO2 87% rising on 3L NC, BGL 112 mg/dL, pupils PEARRL 3 mm.
I auscultate George's lungs: distant breath sounds bilaterally, coarse rhonchi in upper bronchial zones, and expiratory wheezes throughout.

I inspect George's Albuterol MDI: right patient, right medication (Albuterol 90 mcg/puff), right dose (2 puffs), right route (inhalation), unexpired. I attach a spacer chamber to maximize lower airway deposition.

Contacting Medical Control: 'Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. On scene with a 68-year-old male with COPD exacerbation. Vitals: BP 148/88, HR 104, RR 26, SpO2 88% on 3L NC. Coarse rhonchi and wheezes. No contraindications. Requesting authorization to assist patient with 2 puffs of his prescribed Albuterol MDI with spacer.'
Medic 4, authorized: assist patient with 2 puffs Albuterol MDI with spacer, coach breath hold for 10 seconds per puff.
Medical Control, copy and confirm: Authorized for 2 puffs Albuterol MDI with spacer, coaching 10-second breath hold. Candidate out.

George, exhale completely, place your lips tightly around the spacer mouthpiece. When I press the canister, inhale slowly and deeply, then hold your breath for 10 seconds. We deliver puff 1, wait 1 minute, then deliver puff 2.
We assist George to the stretcher, maintain a high-Fowler's (90 degree) seated position, and initiate transport.
George is breathing more comfortably. Rhonchi have mobilized. Repeat vitals: BP 142/84 mmHg, HR 98 bpm, RR 20 breaths/min, SpO2 91% on 3 L/min NC.

ALS Verbal Hand-Off Report: 'This is George Miller, 68M, presenting with an acute COPD/emphysema exacerbation triggered by a 3-day productive respiratory infection. Baseline vitals: BP 148/88, HR 104, RR 26 with prolonged expiration, SpO2 84% on room air (baseline 88-90%), barrel chest, rhonchi and wheezes. We initiated titrated O2 via nasal cannula at 3 L/min (targeting 88-92% SpO2) and assisted with 2 puffs of his prescribed Albuterol MDI with spacer under medical control. Repeat vitals: BP 142/84, HR 98, RR 20, SpO2 91% on 3L NC. Patient is stable, seated upright, and prepped for ALS transport.'
hand_off_report: George Miller, 68M, acute COPD exacerbation secondary to bronchitis. Presenting with barrel chest, pursed-lip breathing, coarse rhonchi, and wheezes. Baseline BP 148/88, HR 104, RR 26, SpO2 84%. Managed with targeted O2 titration at 3 L/min NC (target 88-92%) and 2 puffs Albuterol MDI with spacer per medical control. Failing to give oxygen because of fear of hypoxic drive (NEVER withhold oxygen from a hypoxic patient; titrate to 88-92%).
Failing to use a spacer or coach breath-holding when administering an MDI.
Laying a COPD patient supine (causes severe diaphragmatic mechanical disadvantage).

title: Spontaneous Pneumothorax Transitioning to Tension Pneumothorax

patient.name: Connor Walsh
patient.complaint: Sudden knife-like right-sided chest pain, progressive suffocating dyspnea

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 to Campus Recreation Center, Court 2, for a 21-year-old male basketball player who collapsed with acute chest pain and difficulty breathing.
clues: Classic patient demographic: Tall, thin, young athletic male (rupture of congenital apical subpleural bleb)
Sudden, sharp, pleuritic, knife-like pain localized to one hemithorax (right side) triggered during exertion
UNILATERAL ABSENT BREATH SOUNDS on the affected right side with hyperresonance to percussion
Progression to TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX: Hypotension (BP 88/56), tracheal deviation to the contralateral left side, and jugular venous distension (JVD)

LETHAL TRAP: Bag-valve-mask positive pressure ventilation is STRICTLY CONTRAINDICATED (unless patient is apneic) because positive pressure pumps more air into the pleural space, accelerating tension collapse! Immediate ALS needle decompression required.

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Completely ABSENT on the right side; clear with compensatory tachypnea on the left
baseline_vitals.pain_score: 9 / 10 sharp pleuritic knife pain on every breath

reassessment_vitals.lung_sounds: Right side remains completely absent; tracheal shift palpable to left

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 to Campus Rec Center Court 2, 21-year-old male basketball player collapsed with severe chest pain.
Dispatched to 21M collapsed on court. BSI: gloves, eye protection. Scene safe?
Scene is safe. Teammates are standing back.
Nature of illness: acute pleuritic chest pain / suspected pneumothorax. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately.
General impression: 21-year-old male, tall and thin (6'4", 160 lbs), sitting on bench, leaning sharply to right side, clutching right chest, cyanotic lips. No trauma reported, C-spine not indicated.
Hello, I'm EMT Luke. What is your name and what happened?
Connor... (gasp)... was going up for a rebound... felt a pop in my right lung... now it feels like a knife inside... can't catch breath...
Connor is alert, dyspneic. Airway is patent. Respirations are 32 breaths/min, shallow, with asymmetrical right-sided chest rise. SpO2 is 86%.

OXYGENATION DECISION: I apply high-flow oxygen via Non-Rebreather mask at 15 L/min. I WILL NOT APPLY POSITIVE PRESSURE BVM VENTILATIONS as long as he is breathing spontaneously. Positive pressure would force air into the pleural space and worsen tension.
Checking circulation: radial pulse is 128 bpm, rapid and weak. Skin is pale, cool, and clammy. Blood pressure is 88/56 mmHg. JVD noted in neck veins.
IMMEDIATE LOAD-AND-GO EMERGENCY. Connor has signs of a Tension Pneumothorax with obstructive shock. Partner, obtain baseline vitals while we load to the stretcher.
I auscultate and inspect the chest: What are my lung sounds and tracheal alignment?

Breath sounds are completely absent across the entire right hemithorax with hyperresonance. Left lung sounds clear. You observe slight tracheal deviation to the patient's left and distended neck veins.
This confirms Tension Pneumothorax. The right pleural space is trapping air, collapsing the right lung, shifting the mediastinum, and compressing the vena cava, causing obstructive shock (BP 88/56).
Connor, do you have any allergies or take any medications?
No... no allergies... no meds... never happened before...

Contacting Medical Control / ALS En Route: 'Medic 1 ALS, this is BLS Medic 4 en route to Valley Medical. We have an immediate life-threat: 21-year-old male with a spontaneous Right Tension Pneumothorax. Absent breath sounds right side, tracheal deviation to left, JVD, BP 88/56, HR 128, SpO2 92% on 15L NRB. We need immediate rendezvous for emergency needle chest decompression (thoracostomy). Meet us at 4th and Main.'
Medic 4, copy! Medic 1 is 60 seconds out at 4th and Main. Pull over; we will board your unit with the decompression kit.
We keep Connor in a semi-Fowler's position of comfort, maintain 15L NRB, monitor for loss of consciousness, and pull over at the rendezvous point.

ALS Verbal Hand-Off Report: 'This is Connor Walsh, 21M, tall athletic habitus, suffered sudden spontaneous right pneumothorax playing basketball that has converted to Tension Pneumothorax. Baseline vitals: BP 88/56, HR 128, RR 32, SpO2 86% on room air. Right breath sounds are completely absent, trachea is deviated to the left, and JVD is prominent. We maintained passive 15L NRB and avoided positive pressure. Repeat BP 86/54, HR 132. He is prepped for immediate 14-gauge needle thoracostomy at the second intercostal space midclavicular line.'
ALS enters, performs successful needle decompression with a rush of air, and BP improves to 118/74. Station passed.
hand_off_report: Connor Walsh, 21M, spontaneous right tension pneumothorax with obstructive shock. Sudden 'pop' and pleuritic pain during exertion. Right breath sounds completely absent, hyperresonance, tracheal deviation to left, JVD, BP 88/56, HR 128, SpO2 86%. Maintained on 15L NRB; positive pressure BVM strictly avoided. Direct ALS hand-off for emergent needle decompression.

Failing to recognize tracheal deviation and JVD as signs of tension pneumothorax.
Delaying transport or ALS rendezvous for a tension pneumothorax (patient will arrest without pleural decompression).
Misdiagnosing as an asthma exacerbation and wasting time with Albuterol nebulizers.

title: Acute Massive Pulmonary Embolism (Refractory Hypoxia Trap)

patient.name: Rachel Green
patient.complaint: Sudden suffocating shortness of breath, sharp pleuritic chest pain, dizziness

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to 742 Evergreen Terrace, Apt 3B, for a 34-year-old female in acute severe respiratory distress. Caller states patient suddenly turned blue and feels faint.
clues: High-risk Virchow's Triad history: Recent orthopedic knee surgery (stasis/hypercoagulability) and oral contraceptive use
Sudden onset of sharp, pleuritic chest pain worse on inhalation, accompanied by profound 'air hunger'
CLEAR BILATERAL BREATH SOUNDS on auscultation (the lungs sound deceptively normal because the defect is vascular, not alveolar!)
REFRACTORY HYPOXIA: SpO2 remains stubbornly low (82-84%) despite high-flow 100% oxygen via Non-Rebreather (ventilation-perfusion V/Q mismatch)
Unilateral lower extremity swelling, erythema, and calf tenderness (DVT source)

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 to 742 Evergreen Terrace Apt 3B, 34-year-old female with sudden acute respiratory distress and cyanosis.
Dispatched to 34F with acute respiratory distress. BSI: gloves, eye protection. Is the scene safe?
Nature of illness: acute pulmonary embolism / severe respiratory compromise. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately.
General impression: 34-year-old female on sofa, gasping for air, clutching her right lateral chest, lips cyanotic, post-op knee brace on right leg. No trauma, C-spine not indicated.
Hello, I'm EMT Luke. What is your name and what happened?
Rachel... (pant)... stood up from couch... sudden sharp pain in my chest... feels like I'm suffocating... can't get any air in...
Rachel is alert, oriented, terrified. Airway is patent. Respirations are 32 breaths/min, rapid and gasping. SpO2 is 82%. I apply high-flow oxygen via Non-Rebreather at 15 L/min.
Checking circulation: radial pulse is 134 bpm, rapid and weak. Skin is pale, cool, diaphoretic. BP is 94/62. Priority load-and-go.
Partner, get baseline vitals while I auscultate lungs and check Rachel's legs.
I auscultate Rachel's lungs: What are my breath sounds?
Breath sounds are completely clear and equal bilaterally in all anterior and posterior fields.

CLINICAL PEARL: Clear lung sounds in the presence of severe acute dyspnea, cyanosis, and profound hypoxia (82%) strongly indicates a pulmonary vascular obstruction (PE) rather than an airway or alveolar process.
Rachel, what were you doing when this started?
Just stood up to go to the kitchen... hit me like a lightning bolt 10 minutes ago.
Sharp, stabbing... gets way worse every time I breathe in.
I see a brace on your right leg. Did you have recent surgery or travel?
Had knee arthroscopy 10 days ago... been resting in bed. I also take birth control pills.
I expose and examine both calves: The right calf is visibly swollen, erythematous, warm, and tender to palpation compared to the left.
Vitals: BP 94/62 mmHg, HR 134 bpm, RR 32, SpO2 86% despite 15L NRB, BGL 108 mg/dL, pupils PEARRL 3 mm.

The patient's refractory hypoxia (SpO2 only 86% on 15L NRB) is caused by a massive pulmonary vascular shunt. A large thrombus is blocking blood flow to ventilated alveoli. No BLS medication will dissolve this clot; the patient requires emergent hospital fibrinolytics (tPA) or catheter thrombectomy.
We position Rachel in a semi-Fowler's position, maintain high-flow 15L NRB, keep her calm and warm, and initiate rapid transport.

Recent knee surgery and OCP use. Sudden pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia HR 134, BP 94/62, clear lung sounds, right calf DVT signs, and refractory hypoxia with SpO2 86% on 15L NRB. Requesting immediate CT pulmonary angiogram / ECMO / fibrinolytic team activation at Saint Luke's.'
Medic 4, copy. Saint Luke's ED is notified for acute PE code. Continue high-flow O2 and expedite.
Medical Control, confirmed: Expediting transport to Saint Luke's with PE code active. Candidate out.
Rachel remains tachycardic at 130 bpm. BP 92/60 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 86% on NRB. Lungs remain clear.

ALS Verbal Hand-Off Report: 'This is Rachel Green, 34F, presenting with acute massive pulmonary embolism. Sudden pleuritic chest pain and air hunger 15 minutes ago. High risk profile: right knee surgery 10 days ago, bed rest, and oral contraceptives. Baseline vitals: BP 94/62, HR 134 sinus tachycardia, RR 32, SpO2 82% on room air. Lungs are completely clear bilaterally, and right calf shows swelling and tenderness. Placed on 15L NRB with refractory SpO2 at 86% due to V/Q mismatch. Repeat BP 92/60, HR 130. Patient is ready for emergent CT angiogram and tPA/heparin therapy.'
hand_off_report: Rachel Green, 34F, acute massive pulmonary embolism. Sudden onset stabbing pleuritic chest pain, severe air hunger, and presyncope. Risk factors: recent knee surgery and oral contraceptives. Baseline BP 94/62, HR 134, RR 32, SpO2 82%. Lungs clear bilaterally, right calf DVT noted. Placed on 15L NRB with refractory hypoxia at 86% (V/Q shunt). Repeat BP 92/60, HR 130. Emergency hospital hand-off for CT angiogram and thrombolytics.

Removing high-flow oxygen because SpO2 is not climbing to 100% (maintain 15L NRB to maximize dissolved arterial PaO2).
Delaying transport to search for medications (PE requires definitive hospital fibrinolysis/thrombectomy).
Massaging or aggressively squeezing the tender calf (can dislodge additional emboli into the vena cava).

I approach Tommy very quietly and calmly. I observe saliva actively drooling from his mouth because he cannot swallow.

I initiate Blow-By Oxygen: I have Tommy's mother hold the non-rebreather mask or oxygen tubing 2 inches from Tommy's nose and mouth at 10-15 L/min. Do not force the mask onto his face, which would cause crying and increase airway edema.
Circulation: radial/brachial pulse is 146 bpm, strong. Skin is hot and pale. Cap refill is 2 seconds. Immediate high-priority load-and-go.

Medical Control, confirmed: Transporting directly to Children's with ENT ready. Candidate out.

He takes Eliquis for his irregular heartbeat and lisinopril for blood pressure.

We package Robert with the head of the cot elevated 15 to 30 degrees to reduce intracranial pressure while maintaining cerebral blood flow, and initiate immediate emergency transport to a certified Comprehensive Stroke Center.

Laying the acute stroke patient flat (increases intracranial pressure).

title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) with Kussmaul Breathing

patient.name: Zachary Taylor
patient.complaint: Profound weakness, vomiting, deep rapid panting, severe abdominal pain

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 2 to University Hall, Room 304, for a 19-year-old male with persistent vomiting, extreme weakness, and strange heavy breathing. Caller is his roommate.
clues: Kussmaul Respirations: Deep, rapid, gasping respirations (attempting to blow off volatile carbonic acid / CO2 to compensate for profound metabolic ketoacidosis)
Distinct fruity, sweet, acetone odor on the patient's breath
The Classical '3 P's': Polyuria (excess urination), Polydipsia (unquenchable thirst), and Polyphagia leading to nausea/vomiting
Profound systemic dehydration: Sunken eyes, dry cracked lips, poor skin turgor (tenting), orthostatic hypotension
Fingerstick Blood Glucose Level reads 'HIGH' (>500 mg/dL); requires aggressive ALS IV Normal Saline fluid resuscitation (do NOT give oral fluids or sugar!)

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Clear bilaterally throughout all fields (lungs are compensating, not diseased)

reassessment_vitals.bp: 104/66 mmHg (improving with ALS IV fluid bolus)

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 2 response to University Hall Room 304, 19-year-old male with heavy breathing, vomiting, and weakness.
Dispatched to 19M with respiratory abnormalities and vomiting. BSI: gloves, eye protection, mask. Scene safe?
Scene is safe. Roommate opens the door.
Nature of illness: endocrine emergency / suspected DKA. One patient. Requesting ALS backup for IV rehydration therapy.

General impression: 19-year-old male lying in bed, breathing very deeply and rapidly with audible sighs, flushed cheeks, emesis basin by bed. I smell a distinct sweet, fruity, nail-polish remover scent in the air. C-spine not indicated.
Hello, I'm EMT Luke. Can you tell me your name?
Zach... (deep gasp)... stomach hurts so bad... so thirsty... feel like I'm dying...
Airway is patent, no active emesis. Respirations are 32 breaths/min, abnormally deep and rapid. SpO2 is 97%.
I apply oxygen via nasal cannula at 4 L/min. Checking circulation: radial pulse is 124 bpm, rapid and weak. Skin is warm, dry, with tenting turgor. Oral mucosa is parched.
Partner, please obtain full vitals and an IMMEDIATE blood glucose check while I palpate Zach's abdomen and review his history.
I palpate the abdomen: soft, diffuse mild tenderness across all 4 quadrants, no rigid guarding, no rebound. This is metabolic ketoacidotic ileus.
Vitals: BP 96/60 mmHg, HR 124, RR 32 deep and sighing, SpO2 97%, GLUCOMETER READS 'HI' (>500 mg/dL).
The glucometer reads 'HI' (>500 mg/dL). Zach is in classic Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA). Zach, are you a Type 1 diabetic?
Yeah... diagnosed at age 12... had the flu two days ago and couldn't keep food down, so I stopped taking my insulin...

CLINICAL PATHOPHYSIOLOGY PEARL: When a diabetic gets sick, stress hormones spike blood sugar. Stopping insulin causes the cells to starve, metabolizing fatty acids into ketones, resulting in severe metabolic acidosis. The Kussmaul breathing is the body's respiratory attempt to blow off CO2 to raise blood pH.

Zach is in hypovolemic dehydration from osmotic diuresis (losing 5 to 10 liters of fluid). ORAL FLUIDS ARE STRICTLY WITHHELD due to nausea and vomiting. He requires immediate IV Normal Saline from ALS.
We package Zach supine with legs elevated slightly to support blood pressure, keep him warm, and begin transport to rendezvous with ALS.

Baseline vitals: BP 96/60, HR 124 thready, SpO2 97%, BGL maxed at 'HI' (>500 mg/dL). Lungs clear. Patient kept NPO, placed on 4L NC, and ALS infused 500 mL Normal Saline bolus. Excellent clinical understanding of DKA. Station passed.

title: Status Epilepticus & Post-Ictal Airway Management

patient.name: Marcus Reed
patient.complaint: Continuous generalized tonic-clonic convulsions > 5 minutes without waking

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to City Java, 400 Market Street, for a 28-year-old male actively seizing on the sidewalk. Callers report he has been shaking for over 6 minutes.
clues: Status Epilepticus definition: Continuous generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting > 5 minutes OR recurrent seizures without full recovery of consciousness between episodes
Severe cerebral hypoxia, hyperthermia, and metabolic lactic acidosis developing rapidly
Immediate airway threat: Blood-tinged foamy saliva from lateral tongue biting, trismus (clenched jaw), and sonorous snoring upon cessation of motor activity

CRITICAL AIRWAY CONTRAINDICATION: NEVER force anything between clenched teeth (DO NOT use an Oropharyngeal Airway / OPA). Insert a lubricated Nasopharyngeal Airway (NPA) and perform gentle suctioning!
Immediate ALS request for IV/IN Benzodiazepines (Midazolam / Versed 5-10 mg)

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Coarse upper airway bubbling; bilateral breath sounds present but shallow

reassessment_vitals.lung_sounds: Upper airway clear post-suction; equal aeration
reassessment_vitals.pain_score: Moaning to painful stimuli (P on AVPU)

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 response to City Java, 400 Market Street, 28-year-old male in continuous active seizure.
Dispatched to 28M actively seizing. BSI: gloves, eye protection. Is the scene safe?
Scene is safe. Coffee shop patrons have moved chairs away.
Nature of illness: status epilepticus / neurological life-threat. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately for pharmaceutical seizure termination.

General impression: 28-year-old male on concrete, actively seizing with rhythmic full-body tonic-clonic jerking, teeth clenched, blood-tinged foam at mouth, facial cyanosis. I protect his head with a soft jacket, move hard objects away, and DO NOT restrain his limbs.
After 60 seconds, the convulsions cease. The patient becomes completely flaccid, unresponsive, and begins snoring loudly.
PRIMARY ASSESSMENT: The patient is unresponsive (U on AVPU). Loud sonorous snoring indicates the tongue is occluding the hypopharynx. Blood-tinged foam is in his mouth.
AIRWAY MANAGEMENT PROTOCOL: I perform a modified jaw-thrust maneuver. I prepare the rigid tip suction catheter. I suction the oral cavity for no more than 15 seconds, removing secretions and blood.

AIRWAY ADJUNCT SELECTION: His jaw remains tight with trismus. I WILL NOT FORCE AN OPA BETWEEN HIS TEETH. I select a Nasopharyngeal Airway (NPA), size it from tip of nose to earlobe, lubricate with water-soluble jelly, and insert bevel toward the septum into the right nostril.
NPA passes smoothly. Snoring respirations immediately cease.

How is my patient's breathing? Respirations are 8 breaths/min, extremely shallow, SpO2 is 81%. This is inadequate ventilation. I immediately initiate Bag-Valve-Mask (BVM) ventilations with 100% O2 at 1 breath every 5 to 6 seconds (10-12 breaths/min).

title: Subarachnoid Hemorrhage with Herniation & Cushing's Triad

patient.complaint: Sudden explosive 'thunderclap' headache, projectile vomiting, decreasing LOC

Meningeal irritation signs: Severe nuchal rigidity (stiff neck), photophobia, and projectile vomiting

CUSHING'S TRIAD (The Hallmark of Impending Brain Herniation): 1. Progressive Hypertension with Widening Pulse Pressure (BP 196/60 mmHg); 2. Profound Bradycardia (HR 44 bpm); 3. Irregular Respiratory Pattern (Cheyne-Stokes respirations)
Uncal Herniation Pupillary Sign: Unilateral dilated, non-reactive pupil ('blown pupil')

HERNIATION VENTILATION PROTOCOL: Because the patient exhibits definitive signs of uncal herniation (blown pupil + Cushing's triad + dropping GCS), mild controlled hyperventilation is indicated to induce cerebral vasoconstriction and temporarily lower ICP. I initiate BVM ventilations with 100% O2 at 20 breaths per minute (1 breath every 3 seconds), targeting an EtCO2 of 30-35 mmHg.
I position Patricia on the cot with the head elevated 30 degrees to promote jugular venous drainage and reduce intracranial pressure. I ensure her head and neck remain strictly midline.
IMMEDIATE CODE 3 LOAD-AND-GO TO A COMPREHENSIVE NEUROTRAUMA / NEUROSURGICAL CENTER. We notify Medical Control.

Medic 4, copy. University Trauma neurosurgery is scrubbed and waiting. Expedite transport.

Hyperventilating a head injury patient routinely WITHOUT active signs of herniation (causes excessive vasoconstriction and cerebral ischemia; ONLY hyperventilate if blown pupil/posturing is present!).
Laying a patient with high ICP flat (causes sudden spike in intracranial pressure and accelerates herniation).

Dismissing a 'thunderclap' headache as a routine tension headache or migraine.

title: Severe Systemic Anaphylactic Shock (The Epinephrine Mandate)

patient.name: David Choi
patient.complaint: Acute throat tightening, facial swelling, widespread hives, severe dizziness

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to Bangkok Bistro, 1200 Pacific Highway, for a 29-year-old male having a severe allergic reaction after eating peanut sauce. Caller states patient's throat is closing up.
clues: Multi-system involvement: 1. Cutaneous (generalized urticaria/hives, pruritus); 2. Respiratory (stridor, diffuse bronchospastic wheezing, dyspnea); 3. Cardiovascular (distributive shock / hypotension BP 78/46 mmHg)
Prominent angioedema: Swelling of the lips, tongue, uvula, and periorbital tissue

FIRST-LINE DRUG OF CHOICE: Immediate Intramuscular Epinephrine 0.3 mg (1:1,000) into the anterolateral thigh (EpiPen / auto-injector). Antihistamines (Benadryl) and Albuterol are secondary adjuncts and NEVER replace Epinephrine!

Distributive shock positioning: Lie the patient supine with legs elevated (Trendelenburg/modified) unless respiratory distress forces high-Fowler's; avoid sudden standing (causes fatal 'empty ventricle syndrome')
Biphasic reaction alert: Symptoms can recur 4 to 8 hours later despite initial recovery

reassessment_vitals.bp: 112/70 mmHg (alpha-1 vasoconstriction restoring systemic vascular resistance)
reassessment_vitals.lung_sounds: Stridor completely resolved; wheezing significantly softened
reassessment_vitals.pain_score: 3 / 10 ('My throat opened up, I can breathe again')

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 response to Bangkok Bistro, 29-year-old male with severe peanut anaphylaxis, throat closing.
Dispatched to 29M with severe food anaphylaxis. BSI: gloves, eye protection. Is the scene safe?
Scene is safe. Waitstaff has cleared patrons away.
Nature of illness: severe systemic anaphylactic shock / life-threat. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately for airway protection and secondary meds.

General impression: 29-year-old male sitting on patio chair, gasping for air, massive swelling of lips and eyelids (angioedema), scratching raised red hives (urticaria) across chest and neck, cyanotic lips. No trauma, C-spine not indicated.
Hello, I'm EMT Luke. Can you speak to me?
(High-pitched raspy whisper)... throat... tight... closing... dizzy...
AIRWAY & BREATHING: Airway is critically narrowed by laryngeal angioedema. Inspiratory stridor is audible. Respirations are 30 breaths/min, severely labored. SpO2 is 88%.
CIRCULATION: Radial pulse is 134 bpm, rapid and weak. Skin is hot, flushed, covered in urticaria, and diaphoretic. Cap refill is 3 seconds. Blood pressure is 78/46 mmHg.
IMMEDIATE FIRST-LINE LIFESAVING ACTION: THIS IS SEVERE SYSTEMIC ANAPHYLAXIS WITH DISTRIBUTIVE SHOCK. EPINEPHRINE IS INDICATED IMMEDIATELY. I ask: David, do you have an EpiPen?
(Nods and points weakly to his backpack on the chair).

I retrieve David's auto-injector: Right patient (David Choi), Right drug (Epinephrine Auto-Injector 1:1,000 / 1 mg/mL), Right dose (0.3 mg adult), Right route (Intramuscular), Right time, in date, clear liquid without precipitate.

ADMINISTRATION PROTOCOL: I remove the safety cap, position the auto-injector at a 90-degree angle against the anterolateral aspect of David's thigh (vastus lateralis), push firmly until the spring activates with a click, and hold firmly against the thigh for a full 10 seconds. I then massage the site for 10 seconds.
I apply high-flow oxygen via Non-Rebreather mask at 15 L/min. Partner, obtain full baseline vitals now.
Initial vitals: BP was 78/46 mmHg, HR 134, RR 30, SpO2 88% on room air, BGL 104 mg/dL.

PATIENT POSITIONING WARNING: David is in distributive shock (BP 78/46). If a patient in anaphylaxis sits up or stands suddenly, blood pools in the dilated venous system, starving the heart ('empty ventricle syndrome') and causing sudden cardiac arrest. We place David supine on the cot with his legs elevated 12 inches (modified Trendelenburg).
To the friend: Did David eat peanuts, and has this happened before?
Yes, severe peanut allergy! The curry was supposed to be peanut-free, but he tasted peanut sauce and his throat seized up within 2 minutes.

SECONDARY MEDICATION EVALUATION: For persistent bronchospasm, I prepare an Albuterol nebulizer (2.5 mg) at 6-8 L/min O2. CLINICAL RULE: Albuterol treats lower airway bronchospasm, but it does NOT reverse laryngeal edema or shock. Epinephrine is the sole definitive therapy.

Immediate load-and-go transport. Contacting Medical Control: 'Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. Priority transport with a 29-year-old male with severe systemic anaphylactic shock following peanut exposure. Baseline vitals: BP 78/46, HR 134, RR 30, SpO2 88%, stridor, hives, and facial angioedema. Patient's prescribed Epinephrine auto-injector 0.3 mg IM administered into the lateral thigh at 12:05. Patient placed supine with legs elevated and 15L NRB applied. If systolic BP remains < 90 or stridor recurs after 5 to 10 minutes, I request standing order authorization for a second 0.3 mg Epinephrine dose.'
Medic 4, copy. Second dose of Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM is AUTHORIZED at 5 to 10 minutes if symptoms refractory. Continue rapid transport.
Medical Control, confirmed: Authorized for repeat Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM at 5 to 10 minutes if refractory. Candidate out.
David is breathing much easier. Stridor is completely gone. Facial swelling is beginning to subside. Repeat vitals: BP 112/70 mmHg, HR 118 bpm, RR 20 breaths/min, SpO2 96% on NRB.

The single dose of Epinephrine successfully stimulated alpha-1 vasoconstriction to restore blood pressure to 112/70 mmHg, and beta-2 bronchodilation to relieve laryngeal edema. A second dose is not needed at this time.

ALS / Emergency Department Hand-Off Report: 'This is David Choi, 29M, severe systemic anaphylaxis secondary to peanut ingestion. Rapid onset laryngeal angioedema, inspiratory stridor, diffuse urticaria, and distributive shock. Baseline vitals: BP 78/46, HR 134, RR 30, SpO2 88% on room air. We administered patient's Epinephrine 0.3 mg IM into the anterolateral thigh at 12:05, placed him supine with legs elevated, and applied 15L NRB. Repeat vitals: BP 112/70, HR 118, RR 20, SpO2 96%. Stridor has resolved and wheezing is minimal. Patient requires mandatory 6 to 8 hour hospital observation for biphasic anaphylactic recurrence, along with IV steroids and H1/H2 antihistamines.'
hand_off_report: David Choi, 29M, acute systemic anaphylactic shock triggered by peanut ingestion. Presenting with facial angioedema, inspiratory stridor, diffuse urticaria, and distributive shock. Allowing a hypotensive anaphylactic patient to stand or sit upright (causes fatal cardiovascular collapse via 'empty ventricle syndrome').
Injecting Epinephrine subcutaneously instead of Intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh (vastus lateralis has the fastest absorption rate).
Failing to monitor for biphasic anaphylactic recurrence or allowing the patient to sign a refusal after initial recovery.

differential_matrix.impact: Inhaled bronchodilators primary; non-allergic etiology.

differential_matrix.clue: Bradycardia (HR < 60), pallor, sudden fainting after emotional stress, NO hives, rapid recovery when flat

title: Exertional Heat Stroke (The 'Cool First, Transport Second' Mandate)

patient.name: Brandon Cole
patient.complaint: Collapse during high-intensity football drills, delirium, hot dry skin

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to City Stadium, field level, for a 24-year-old athlete who collapsed during practice. Athletic trainer reports core temp > 105°F and seizure-like twitching.
clues: Profound Central Nervous System (CNS) Dysfunction: Confusion, delirium, bizarre behavior, ataxia, or coma/seizures
Core body temperature > 104°F (40°C) measured via rectal thermometer
Skin condition: Hot, flushed, and either profusely sweating (early exertional) or bone dry (cessation of sweating due to hypothalamic thermoregulatory failure)

CRITICAL TREATMENT PARADOX: 'COOL FIRST, TRANSPORT SECOND!' Active, aggressive whole-body cold-water immersion (or ice packs to neck, axillae, and groin) TAKES PRECEDENCE over immediate ambulance transport. Transporting before cooling leads to permanent brain damage and death!
Cool aggressively until core temperature reaches 102°F (38.9°C), then discontinue cooling to prevent rebound hypothermia

baseline_vitals.pain_score: Unresponsive to verbal, moaning to painful stimuli (P on AVPU)

Scene is safe. Heat index is 102°F with 80% humidity on the turf. Athletic trainer is on scene.
Nature of illness: exertional heat stroke / true environmental life-threat. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately.

(Incoherent groans, thrashing limbs, eyes roll back).

We just checked his rectal temperature with our certified medical probe: it is 105.4°F.

I instruct the team: Strip all remaining clothing down to underwear. If a cold-water immersion tub is available, immerse the patient up to the neck in ice water with head supported. Partner, monitor rectal temperature continuously. We will cool him aggressively until his core temperature drops to 102°F (38.9°C), then remove him to prevent hypothermic overshoot.
Partner, check BGL to ensure hypoglycemia is not contributing to altered mental status.
After 8 minutes in the cold water tub, Brandon's rectal temperature reaches 102.0°F. He begins shivering and answers simple questions.
Target temperature of 102°F reached! Remove Brandon from the ice tub immediately, dry him with clean towels, place him on the stretcher, and begin rapid transport to the emergency department.

Patient is now responsive to voice. High-flow O2 applied. Requesting ICU / rhabdomyolysis team alert at Saint Mary's ED.'
Medic 4, outstanding management. Saint Mary's ED is ready for IV hydration and renal monitoring for myoglobinuria.
Medical Control, confirmed: Transporting to Saint Mary's with rhabdomyolysis protocol active. Candidate out.
Brandon is alert to verbal stimuli. Repeat vitals: BP 110/68 mmHg, HR 114 bpm, RR 20, SpO2 99% on NRB, core temp 101.8°F.

Failing to remove athletic pads and heavy equipment immediately.
Administering oral fluids to a semi-conscious or delirious heat stroke patient (severe aspiration risk).

differential_matrix.impact: Requires IV Dantrolene; specialized pharmacologic therapy.

title: Severe Accidental Hypothermia (The 45-Second Pulse Check)

patient.name: William MacLeod
patient.setting: Under concrete bridge overpass in freezing rain
patient.complaint: Found motionless, rigid, soaked in freezing water, barely breathing

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to River Road bridge, 52-year-old male found unresponsive by outreach workers. Ambient temperature 34°F with sleet and freezing rain.
clues: Severe Hypothermia stage (Core Body Temperature < 82.4°F / 28°C): Cessation of shivering, extreme muscular rigidity, unresponsiveness
Profound physiological depression: Extreme bradycardia (HR 24-28 bpm), bradypnea (RR 4-6 breaths/min), unrecordable blood pressure

MANDATORY NREMT EXAM RULE: Auscultate the carotid pulse for a FULL 30 TO 45 SECONDS before concluding cardiac arrest! (A hypothermic pulse is exceptionally slow, weak, and easily missed; starting chest compressions on a heart with an organized rhythm triggers fatal Ventricular Fibrillation!)
EXTREME GENTLE HANDLING: Rough movement, jostling, or aggressive airway manipulation triggers intractable, refractory V-Fib in an irritable hypothermic myocardium
'A patient is NOT dead until they are WARM AND DEAD!' Passive core rewarming, warm humidified O2, bypass local ED for ECMO/Cardiopulmonary bypass center if indicated

baseline_vitals.hr: 26 bpm (profound sinus bradycardia, confirmed after 45-second carotid auscultation)
baseline_vitals.spo2: Unrecordable due to intense peripheral vasoconstriction
baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Diminished bilaterally, no rales
baseline_vitals.temp: 81.4°F (27.4°C) measured via low-reading esophageal/rectal core probe
baseline_vitals.pupils: Fixed, dilated at 5 mm (mimics clinical death, but reversible with rewarming!)

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 response to River Road bridge overpass, 52-year-old male unresponsive in freezing sleet.
Dispatched to 52M found in freezing conditions. BSI: gloves, eye protection, cold-weather protective gear. Scene safe?
Scene is safe. Sleet is falling. Patient is lying in a freezing puddle under the bridge.
Nature of illness: severe accidental hypothermia / environmental arrest risk. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately.
General impression: 52-year-old male lying motionless in wet clothes, skin is ice cold and waxy pale, no active shivering, extremities are stiff and rigid. C-spine stabilized gently.
PRIMARY ASSESSMENT: Patient is unresponsive (U on AVPU). Respirations are 4 breaths/min, extremely slow and shallow. Airway is clear of vomit.

CRITICAL NREMT MANDATE: THE 45-SECOND PULSE CHECK. In severe hypothermia, metabolic rate drops by 50% or more. A pulse may only beat once every 2 to 3 seconds. I place my fingers on the carotid artery and palpate continuously for a FULL 30 TO 45 SECONDS. Evaluator, what do I feel over 45 seconds?
At 38 seconds, you feel a very faint, slow, rhythmic carotid pulse beating at roughly 26 beats per minute.
PULSE PRESENT AT 26 BPM. DO NOT BEGIN CHEST COMPRESSIONS! Initiating CPR on a hypothermic heart with an organized rhythm will trigger fatal, intractable Ventricular Fibrillation.
GENTLE HANDLING MANDATE: The hypothermic myocardium is exquisitely irritable. We must move William with EXTREME GENTLENESS. Any rough jostling or sudden positional changes can induce cardiac arrest.

VENTILATION & OXYGENATION: With a respiratory rate of 4 breaths/min, I gently assist ventilations using a Bag-Valve-Mask with 100% warm, humidified oxygen at a slow rate of 6 to 8 breaths per minute. Do not hyperventilate, which causes alkalosis and triggers V-Fib.

REWARMING PROTOCOL: Immediately remove all wet clothing by cutting it off gently. Do not rub the skin. Wrap the patient in dry blankets, plastic vapor barrier, and apply active heating pads ONLY to the core (axillae, groin, and anterior chest). DO NOT rewarm the arms or legs, which causes 'core temperature afterdrop' and rewarming shock.
Vitals: BP 64/40 mmHg (doppler), HR 26 bpm, RR 4 assisted to 8, temp via low-reading core probe is 81.4°F (27.4°C), BGL 68 mg/dL, pupils fixed and dilated.

Pupils are fixed and dilated; in hypothermia, this is a reversible physiologic depression, NOT brain death. 'The patient is not dead until warm and dead!' We load William onto the stretcher with extreme care and heat the ambulance patient compartment to 85°F.

Contacting Medical Control: 'Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. Priority transport with a 52-year-old male with severe accidental hypothermia. Core temperature 81.4°F. Presenting in profound coma, rigid, carotid pulse 26 bpm verified via 45-second check, RR 4 assisted gently via warm humidified BVM at 8/min. Wet clothing cut away, truncal rewarming active. Handled with extreme gentleness. Requesting bypass to University Hospital ECMO / Cardiopulmonary Bypass Center for extracorporeal rewarming.'
Medic 4, exceptional management. University Hospital ECMO perfusion team is activated. Transport code 3, maintain gentle handling.
Medical Control, confirmed: Transporting to University Hospital ECMO center with gentle handling. Candidate out.
Patient remains motionless and rigid. Carotid pulse remains stable at 30 bpm. BP 72/46 mmHg, RR 8 assisted, core temp rising to 83.0°F.

Hospital / ECMO Resuscitation Hand-Off Report: 'This is William MacLeod, 52M, severe accidental hypothermia secondary to environmental exposure in freezing rain. Initial core temp 81.4°F. Found unresponsive, rigid, fixed dilated pupils, and profound bradypnea (RR 4). Carotid pulse verified at 26 bpm after a continuous 45-second check; CPR was deliberately withheld to protect the irritable myocardium from ventricular fibrillation. Wet clothes cut away, passive and active truncal warming applied, gentle BVM ventilations delivered with warm humidified 100% O2. Repeat core temp 83.0°F, HR 30, BP 72/46. Patient is prepped for direct femoral cannulation and ECMO rewarming.'

Rewarming the extremities with hot water or heat packs before the core ('rewarming shock' and 'afterdrop' shunts cold, acidotic blood to the heart, causing arrest).
Pronouncing a hypothermic patient dead in the field ('A patient is not dead until warm and dead').
Hyperventilating the patient with cold dry air.
