title: Severe Opioid Overdose with Respiratory Depression

patient.name: Tyler Bennett
patient.complaint: Found slumped over toilet, blue lips, barely breathing

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to Burger Barn, 600 Commercial Blvd, for a 26-year-old male found unresponsive on the bathroom floor. Caller states patient is turning purple and not breathing.
clues: The Classical Opioid Toxidrome Triad: 1. Central Nervous System Depression (Coma / Unresponsive); 2. Severe Respiratory Depression / Apnea (RR 4 breaths/min, shallow); 3. Miosis (Pinpoint, constricted pupils < 1 mm)
Peripheral cyanosis, cool clammy skin, and sonorous/agonal upper airway breathing

MANDATORY VENTILATION FIRST SEQUENCE: VENTILATE BEFORE NALOXONE! An acutely hypoxic brain is prone to lethal cardiac arrest; you must deliver 2 minutes of Bag-Valve-Mask ventilations with 100% O2 BEFORE administering Naloxone!

Titrated Naloxone (Narcan) Administration: Administer 0.4 to 2.0 mg Intranasally (IN). The goal of Naloxone is RESTORING ADEQUATE SPONTANEOUS BREATHING (RR > 10, SpO2 > 94%), NOT waking the patient up into violent acute opioid withdrawal or triggering flash pulmonary edema!
Short half-life awareness: Naloxone half-life (30-90 minutes) is much shorter than most opioids (Fentanyl, Methadone); risk of re-sedation and secondary apnea

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Shallow aeration, faint bilateral air entry, no rales
baseline_vitals.pupils: Pinpoint, constricted to < 1 mm, non-reactive to light

reassessment_vitals.pain_score: Responds to voice, confused and groggy (V on AVPU)

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 to Burger Barn, 600 Commercial Blvd, 26-year-old male unresponsive, turning blue in restroom.
Dispatched to 26M unresponsive in public restroom. BSI: gloves, eye protection. Scene safe? I look for uncapped needles or fentanyl powder before stepping inside.
Scene is safe. You see a lighter and an uncapped syringe on the sink counter. No powders airborne.
Nature of illness: toxicologic overdose / respiratory arrest. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately.

General impression: 26-year-old male slumped between toilet and partition, cyanotic lips and fingernails, flaccid, making agonal gurgling sounds. C-spine: no trauma witnessed, but I maintain neutral alignment during extrication.
PRIMARY ASSESSMENT: Sir, can you hear me? (sternal rub performed). Patient is unresponsive (U on AVPU).
AIRWAY & BREATHING: Airway is open. Agonal gurgling noted. Respirations are 4 breaths/min, severely shallow. SpO2 is 74% on room air. Carotid pulse is 54 bpm, weak.

CRITICAL NREMT PROTOCOL CHECKPOINT: OXYGENATION PRECEDES NALOXONE! I WILL NOT DELAY VENTILATIONS TO SEARCH FOR NARCAN. The brain is suffering from severe hypoxemic ischemia. Partner, prepare Naloxone while I immediately initiate BVM ventilations.

I insert a lubricated Nasopharyngeal Airway (NPA), achieve an airtight mask seal using the E-C clamp technique, and deliver 1 ventilation every 5 seconds using a Bag-Valve-Mask connected to 100% O2 with reservoir for 2 full minutes.
With 2 minutes of effective BVM ventilations, chest rises symmetrically. SpO2 rises from 74% to 92%. Radial pulse is 72 bpm.
I examine pupils and skin: Pupils are pinpoint (< 1 mm, pinpoint miosis). Track marks noted on left antecubital fossa. BGL check reads 92 mg/dL.
The patient exhibits classic opioid toxidrome (coma, respiratory arrest, pinpoint pupils). Now that the patient is oxygenated, I administer Naloxone (Narcan).

I inspect Naloxone: Right patient, Right medication (Naloxone 4 mg/0.1 mL nasal spray or 2 mg/2 mL with mucosal atomizer), Right dose (titrating 1 mg per nostril, total 2 mg IN), Right route (Intranasal), Right time, in date. I administer 1 mg into the right nostril, and 1 mg into the left nostril.

CLINICAL GOAL OF NALOXONE: I continue gentle BVM ventilations while awaiting medication absorption (2 to 3 minutes). The objective is to restore adequate spontaneous breathing (RR > 10), NOT to precipitate violent withdrawal, vomiting, or acute pulmonary edema.
At 3 minutes post-IN Naloxone, Tyler takes a sudden deep spontaneous gasp. He begins breathing on his own at 14 breaths per minute. His eyelids flutter open.
I remove the BVM mask, maintain high-flow O2 via non-rebreather or nasal cannula, and place Tyler in the recovery position on the stretcher to guard against aspiration if nausea occurs.
(Groggily)... what happened... why are you in my face...
Tyler, you're safe. You overdosed in the restroom and stopped breathing. We gave you medicine to help you breathe. Just rest and take deep breaths.
Vitals: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, RR 14 regular and unassisted, SpO2 97% on room air, pupils 3 mm reactive, BGL 92 mg/dL.

PATIENT REFUSAL WARNING: Tyler states he wants to walk away. I advise him: 'Tyler, Naloxone wears off in 30 to 60 minutes. The heroin/fentanyl in your system lasts 4 to 8 hours. When this medicine wears off, you will stop breathing again and could die in your sleep. You must be monitored at the hospital.'

Contacting Medical Control: 'Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. On scene with a 26-year-old male with confirmed acute opioid overdose. Initial presentation: apneic (RR 4), SpO2 74%, pinpoint pupils, unresponsive. Successfully pre-oxygenated via BVM for 2 minutes, then administered 2 mg Naloxone IN. Spontaneous breathing restored at 14 breaths/min, SpO2 97%, alert to voice. Patient is cooperative and agreeable to hospital transport.'
Medic 4, copy. Transport to Memorial ED for extended toxicologic monitoring.
Tyler remains conscious. RR 14, HR 84, BP 120/74, SpO2 98%.

Hospital Hand-Off Report: 'This is Tyler Bennett, 26M, acute opioid overdose. Found unresponsive in public restroom with paraphernalia. Initial vitals: profound respiratory arrest (RR 4), SpO2 74%, HR 54, pinpoint pupils < 1 mm. Resuscitation sequence: Immediate 2 minutes of BVM ventilations with 100% O2 raising SpO2 to 92%, followed by 2 mg Naloxone IN (1 mg per naris). Spontaneous breathing restored within 3 minutes. Baseline BGL 92 mg/dL. Repeat vitals: BP 118/72, HR 86, RR 14 spontaneous, SpO2 97%. Patient is awake, cooperative, and requires continuous observation due to risk of secondary respiratory arrest once Naloxone metabolizes.'
Flawless prioritization of ventilations over medication. Station passed.
hand_off_report: Tyler Bennett, 26M, severe opioid overdose. Found unresponsive, cyanotic, pinpoint pupils, agonal respirations (RR 4, SpO2 74%). Delivered 2 minutes BVM positive pressure ventilation with 100% O2 first, followed by 2 mg Naloxone IN. Spontaneous respirations restored at 14 breaths/min, SpO2 97%, HR 86, BP 118/72. Monitored in recovery position. Hospital observation required due to mismatch between Naloxone half-life and opioid duration.

Slamming excessive Naloxone (e.g. 4-8 mg IV rapidly) causing acute projectile vomiting, flash pulmonary edema, and combative withdrawal.
Allowing an overdose patient who wakes up to sign a refusal without extensive counseling regarding lethal secondary re-sedation.
Failing to check blood glucose in an unresponsive patient with suspected overdose.
Failing to sweep the scene for uncapped needles or fentanyl dust before kneeling.

differential_matrix.impact: Oral or IV glucose indicated; Naloxone ineffective.

differential_matrix.impact: Neurosurgical emergency; fatal brainstem hemorrhage.

title: Organophosphate Toxicity / Cholinergic Toxidrome (SLUDGEM)

patient.name: Carlos Ramirez
patient.complaint: Drenched in sweat, vomiting, diarrhea, wheezing, massive saliva drooling

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to Valley Orchards, Barn 3, for a 45-year-old agricultural worker who collapsed while spraying pesticides. Caller reports worker is covered in fluid and gasping for air.
clues: The Classical SLUDGEM Cholinergic Mnemonic: Salivation (massive drooling), Lacrimation (tears streaming), Urination (incontinence), Defecation (diarrhea), Gastrointestinal cramping, Emesis (projectile vomiting), Miosis (pinpoint pupils)
The 'Killer B's' (The True Life-Threats in Cholinergic Poisoning): Bronchorrhea (drowning in copious pulmonary secretions), Bronchospasm (severe diffuse wheezing), and Bradycardia (HR 42 bpm)

CRITICAL PROVIDER SAFETY / HAZMAT RULE: SCENE SAFETY & DECONTAMINATION FIRST! Organophosphates are absorbed through intact skin. EMTs MUST wear Level C/B chemical PPE. The patient MUST be completely stripped of contaminated clothing and decontaminated with soap and water BEFORE entering the ambulance!
Airway management priority: Aggressive, continuous rigid suctioning of the copious frothy airway secretions
Immediate ALS intercept for massive doses of Atropine (antimuscarinic) and Pralidoxime (2-PAM / acetylcholinesterase reactivator)

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Diffuse, coarse, wet bubbling throughout all lung fields (bronchorrhea) with high-pitched wheezing
baseline_vitals.pupils: Pinpoint, constricted to < 1 mm (miosis), tears flowing from eyes

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 response to Valley Orchards, 45-year-old pesticide sprayer collapsed in barn, covered in secretions.

Dispatched to pesticide exposure. BSI & SCENE SAFETY HAZMAT ALERT: Organophosphates readily absorb through rescuers' skin and produce secondary contamination. I don full chemical protective PPE (gloves, eye protection, respirator, splash gown). Where is the patient located?
Orchard workers dragged him outside the barn onto the gravel driveway. A pesticide tank marked 'Chlorpyrifos Organophosphate' is leaking nearby.

CRITICAL SAFETY CHECKPOINT: DECONTAMINATION PRIOR TO TRANSPORT. The patient CANNOT be loaded into the closed ambulance box while covered in organophosphates. His contaminated clothing must be cut away and bagged immediately, and he must undergo copious water washing outside.

With assistance from rural fire hazmat, the patient's clothing is completely stripped, double-bagged, and his skin is washed down with copiously running water. He is wrapped in clean tarps and moved to the warm zone.

PRIMARY ASSESSMENT: Carlos is semiconscious (V on AVPU). Saliva is literally pouring from his mouth, tears streaming down his face, and his pants are soiled with urine and liquid stool. Pinpoint pupils noted.

AIRWAY & THE KILLER B's: Carlos's airway is gurgling violently. He is drowning in his own pulmonary secretions (bronchorrhea). I insert a rigid Yankauer suction tip and suction aggressively and continuously.
Respirations are 28 breaths/min, severely labored, with audible wet bubbling. SpO2 is 82%. I apply high-flow oxygen via Non-Rebreather at 15 L/min with suction constantly ready.
Circulation: radial pulse is 42 bpm, profoundly bradycardic and weak. Skin is cool, pale, drenched in sweat. BP is 90/56 mmHg.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY VERBALIZED: Organophosphates permanently inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing massive accumulation of acetylcholine across all muscarinic and nicotinic synapses. The fatal threats are the Killer B's: Bronchorrhea, Bronchospasm, and Bradycardia.

DEFINITIVE TREATMENT: Carlos requires immediate high-dose Atropine (2 to 4 mg IV/IM, doubled every 5 minutes until pulmonary secretions dry) and Pralidoxime (2-PAM 1-2 g) to reactivate the enzyme. I call for ALS intercept immediately.

Contacting Medical Control / ALS Rendezvous: 'Medic 1 ALS, this is EMT Candidate on BLS Medic 4 en route. We have a severe Organophosphate Cholinergic Crisis: 45-year-old agricultural worker fully decontaminated. Presenting with massive SLUDGEM symptoms, severe bronchorrhea, HR 42, BP 90/56, SpO2 82% on 15L NRB. We have active suction running continuously. We need an immediate ALS intercept for high-dose Atropine (minimum 2-4 mg) and 2-PAM. Intercept at Highway 12 Milepost 4.'
Medic 4, Medic 1 is 2 minutes out with Atropine prefilled syringes in hand.
ALS boards your ambulance. Paramedic administers 2 mg of Atropine IV immediately, followed by another 2 mg 3 minutes later.
Carlos's copious oral bubbling begins drying up. Heart rate climbs from 42 to 68 bpm. Bronchial secretions diminish. Repeat vitals: BP 104/64 mmHg, HR 68 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 94% on NRB.

CLINICAL ENDPOINT OF ATROPINE: The hallmark endpoint of adequate atropinization is the CLEARING OF PULMONARY SECRETIONS and resolution of bronchorrhea, NOT the dilation of pupils or heart rate. The lungs are clearing.

Hospital / HazMat ED Hand-Off Report: 'This is Carlos Ramirez, 45M, acute organophosphate pesticide poisoning (Chlorpyrifos). Initial presentation: full SLUDGEM toxidrome (salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramps, emesis, miosis) with fatal Killer B's: massive bronchorrhea, bronchospasm, and severe bradycardia (HR 42, SpO2 82%). Decontamination protocol completed on scene (clothing stripped, bagged, skin copiously irrigated). Managed with continuous suction, 15L NRB, and ALS administered 4 mg Atropine IV. Repeat vitals: BP 104/64, HR 68, RR 22, SpO2 94% with drying pulmonary secretions. Patient is prepped for IV Pralidoxime (2-PAM) infusion and ICU toxicology admission.'
Flawless HazMat awareness and cholinergic management. Station passed.
hand_off_report: Carlos Ramirez, 45M, acute organophosphate cholinergic crisis. Presented with full SLUDGEM toxidrome, pinpoint miosis, severe bronchorrhea, and bradycardia (HR 42, BP 90/56, SpO2 82%). Completed full field decontamination before transport. Managed with aggressive airway suctioning, 15L NRB, and 4 mg IV Atropine via ALS. Repeat vitals BP 104/64, HR 68, RR 22, SpO2 94% with drying of secretions. Prepped for 2-PAM infusion.
critical_traps: Entering the scene or transporting the patient without PPE and without performing decontamination (causes secondary poisoning of EMS providers and closes the ambulance/ED).
Failing to aggressively suction copious bronchorrhea (patient will drown in their own secretions).
Using pupil dilation rather than drying of lung secretions as the benchmark for Atropine dosing.
Treating organophosphate wheezing as asthma and giving only Albuterol (Albuterol does not treat the muscarinic crisis).
Failing to notify the receiving hospital that a contaminated HazMat patient is arriving.

differential_matrix.impact: Naloxone indicated; Atropine ineffective.

differential_matrix.clue: Tachycardia (HR > 140), hypertension, dilated pupils (mydriasis), extreme agitation
differential_matrix.impact: Opposite toxidrome; cooling and benzodiazepines indicated.

differential_matrix.clue: Wet crackles and pink sputum, but normal pupils, NO diarrhea, NO lacrimation, high BP
differential_matrix.impact: CPAP + Nitroglycerin indicated.

title: Acute Peritonitis Secondary to Ruptured Appendicitis

patient.name: Jacob Miller
patient.complaint: Severe diffuse abdominal pain, high fever, rigid board-like belly, vomiting

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 2 to 415 West End Avenue, Apt 2A, for a 31-year-old male with severe unbearable stomach pain and persistent vomiting for 24 hours.
clues: Progression of Appendiceal Pain: Began 24 hours ago as dull, crampy periumbilical pain; migrated to the Right Lower Quadrant (McBurney's Point); then suddenly became severe, diffuse, and excruciating following rupture
THE HALLMARK OF PERITONITIS: Involuntary Guarding and a RIGID, BOARD-LIKE ABDOMEN (the abdominal wall musculature contracts into a rock-hard spasm to protect the inflamed peritoneum)
Rebound Tenderness (Blumberg's Sign): Pain is far worse upon the sudden RELEASE of deep palpation than during the pressing phase
Systemic inflammatory response / early septic shock: High fever (102.8°F), tachycardia (HR 122 bpm), and hypotension (BP 92/56 mmHg)
POSITION OF COMFORT: Transport the patient supine with knees flexed toward the chest (relaxes abdominal wall tension); KEEP STRICTLY NPO (no water/food) for emergency surgery

baseline_vitals.rr: 24 breaths/min (rapid, shallow, splinting against diaphragmatic movement)
baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Clear bilaterally; shallow excursions

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 2 response to 415 West End Ave Apt 2A, 31-year-old male with severe abdominal pain and fever.
Dispatched to 31M with severe abdominal pain. BSI: gloves, eye protection, mask. Scene safe?
Scene is safe. Girlfriend opens the apartment door.
Nature of illness: acute surgical abdomen / peritonitis / sepsis. One patient. Requesting ALS backup for IV fluid resuscitation and analgesia.

General impression: 31-year-old male lying curled on his right side in fetal position with knees pulled to chest, grimacing, moaning, flushed and shivering from fever. No trauma, C-spine not indicated.
Hello Jacob, I'm EMT Luke. Don't try to move. Tell me what's going on.
My stomach... hurts so bad I can't even breathe... any tiny bump or movement kills me...
Airway is patent. Respirations are 24 breaths/min, shallow because taking a deep breath moves his diaphragm and causes severe peritoneal irritation. SpO2 is 96%.

I apply oxygen via nasal cannula at 4 L/min. Checking circulation: radial pulse is 122 bpm, rapid and weak. Skin is hot, flushed, and diaphoretic. BP is 92/56. High-priority load-and-go surgical emergency.
Partner, get a full set of vitals including temperature and BGL while I examine Jacob's abdomen.
Jacob, where did this pain start and where is it now?
Started yesterday around my belly button... then last night it moved down into my lower right side... then two hours ago I had a sudden pop and the pain exploded everywhere!
ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION PROTOCOL: I inspect, then auscultate, then palpate. I palpate the painful area LAST. When I touch the abdomen: What do I feel?

Bowel sounds are completely absent (paralytic ileus). Upon palpation, the entire abdominal wall is rigid and board-like with involuntary spasm. When you release pressure, Jacob screams in agony (severe rebound tenderness / Blumberg's sign).

CRITICAL CLINICAL DIAGNOSIS: Acute peritonitis secondary to ruptured appendicitis. The spill of infected bowel contents into the peritoneal cavity has caused chemical and bacterial peritonitis and septic shock (BP 92/56, HR 122, Temp 102.8°F).

PATIENT MANAGEMENT MANDATES: 1. KEEP STRICTLY NPO (no sips of water, no oral medications) for emergent exploratory laparotomy; 2. Position of comfort: supine with knees bent (flexed) and pillows under knees to relax abdominal tension; 3. Handle the stretcher with extreme gentleness—every pothole vibrates the inflamed peritoneum.
Vitals: BP 92/56 mmHg, HR 122, RR 24 shallow, SpO2 96%, Temp 102.8°F (39.3°C), BGL 110 mg/dL.

Contacting Medical Control / ALS Rendezvous: 'Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. Priority transport with a 31-year-old male with acute peritonitis from ruptured appendicitis. Periumbilical to RLQ migration followed by diffuse rupture 2 hours ago. Rigid board-like abdomen, positive rebound tenderness, absent bowel sounds. Septic shock vitals: BP 92/56, HR 122, Temp 102.8°F. Patient kept NPO, knees flexed, 4L NC applied. Rendezvousing with ALS for IV Normal Saline bolus and broad-spectrum antibiotics alert.'
Medic 4, copy. Rendezvous approved. General Surgery at St. Anthony's is alerted for emergency laparotomy.
ALS boards and initiates a 1,000 mL Normal Saline IV bolus. Repeat vitals: BP 96/60 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, RR 20, SpO2 99%.

General Surgery / Trauma Hand-Off Report: 'This is Jacob Miller, 31M, acute peritonitis secondary to ruptured appendicitis. 24-hour symptom progression from periumbilical ache to RLQ McBurney's point, culminating in sudden rupture and diffuse agony 2 hours ago. Physical exam: rigid board-like abdominal wall, involuntary guarding, positive rebound tenderness, absent bowel sounds. Early septic shock vitals: BP 92/56, HR 122, Temp 102.8°F, RR 24 shallow. Patient maintained strictly NPO, positioned with knees flexed, and ALS initiated 1-liter IV saline bolus. Repeat BP 96/60, HR 116. Patient is ready for emergent surgical appendectomy and peritoneal washout.'
Flawless acute abdomen assessment. Station passed.
hand_off_report: Jacob Miller, 31M, acute peritonitis secondary to ruptured appendicitis with early septic shock. Pain migrated from periumbilical to RLQ before diffusing. Physical exam revealed involuntary guarding, board-like abdominal rigidity, and severe rebound tenderness. Baseline BP 92/56, HR 122, Temp 102.8°F, RR 24. Kept strictly NPO, transported with knees flexed, 4L NC, and ALS IV crystalloid resuscitation. Repeat BP 96/60, HR 116. Direct hand-off for emergent surgical laparotomy.

Palpating the most painful area first (causes severe voluntary guarding and skews the rest of the physical exam).
Transporting with legs completely extended flat (increases abdominal wall tension and worsens peritoneal agony).
Failing to recognize peritonitis and sepsis in a hypotensive, febrile patient with abdominal pain.
Rough driving or bumping the cot carelessly (causes intolerable peritoneal vibration pain).

title: Ruptured Ectopic Pregnancy with Hemorrhagic Shock

patient.name: Jessica Sanchez
patient.complaint: Sudden tearing lower abdominal pain, syncope, left shoulder tip pain

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to Metro Plaza, Suite 400, for a 27-year-old female who collapsed in the breakroom. Co-workers state she is pale, sweating, and complained of agonizing pelvic pain.
clues: Classic Patient Demographic: Any female of childbearing age (12 to 50 years) presenting with lower abdominal or pelvic pain MUST be considered pregnant until proven otherwise!
History of missed menstrual period (amenorrhea for 6 to 8 weeks) with sudden, unilateral, tearing lower quadrant pelvic pain
KEHR'S SIGN (The Hallmark of Hemoperitoneum): Referred sharp pain to the LEFT SHOULDER TIP caused by blood accumulating under the diaphragm and irritating the phrenic nerve (C3-C5)
Decompensated Hemorrhagic Shock: Hypotension (BP 82/48 mmHg), marked tachycardia (HR 128 bpm), cold clammy pale skin, and syncope

CRITICAL PROTOCOL: Immediate high-flow O2, thermal conservation, rapid load-and-go to an OB/GYN surgical trauma center, notify receiving facility of ruptured ectopic pregnancy requiring emergent laparoscopy/salpingostomy

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Clear bilaterally
baseline_vitals.pain_score: 10 / 10 tearing pelvic pain radiating to left shoulder

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 response to Metro Plaza Suite 400, 27-year-old female collapsed with severe pelvic pain.
Dispatched to 27F with acute pelvic pain and syncope. BSI: gloves, eye protection. Scene safe?
Scene is safe. Co-workers are gathered around.
Nature of illness: gynecologic / hemorrhagic life-threat. One patient. Requesting ALS backup immediately.
General impression: 27-year-old female on floor, curled on her left side, clutching her lower abdomen, skin is pale, cool, and clammy. No fall trauma reported, C-spine not indicated.
Jessica, can you hear me? I'm EMT Luke.
(Weakly)... yes... awful pain in my stomach... and my left shoulder hurts so bad...
Airway is patent. Respirations are 26 breaths/min, rapid and shallow. SpO2 is 94%. I apply high-flow oxygen via Non-Rebreather at 15 L/min.
Circulation: radial pulse is 128 bpm, rapid and thready. Skin is pale, cold, and drenched in sweat. Cap refill is 3.5 seconds. BP is 82/48 mmHg.
IMMEDIATE CRITICAL LOAD-AND-GO EMERGENCY. Jessica is in decompensated hemorrhagic shock. Partner, obtain baseline vitals immediately while we move her to the cot.
Jessica, when was your last menstrual period, and is there any chance you could be pregnant?
I missed my period about six weeks ago... took a home test last week and it was positive... was waiting to see my OB next week...
Did you have any vaginal bleeding or spotting today?
Just a tiny bit of dark spotting this morning, then sudden tearing pain on my left side 15 minutes ago, and then I fainted.

The vaginal spotting is minimal because the hemorrhage is inside the abdominal cavity! The left shoulder pain (Kehr's sign) is diaphragmatic blood irritating the phrenic nerve.
I examine the abdomen gently: lower quadrants are tender with guarding, especially on the left. No visible external vaginal hemorrhage.
Vitals: BP 82/48 mmHg, HR 128 thready, RR 26, SpO2 94% on room air, BGL 98 mg/dL, pupils PEARRL 4 mm.

title: Imminent Childbirth with Prolapsed Umbilical Cord

patient.name: Maria Martinez
patient.complaint: Full-term labor, membranes ruptured, states 'something is coming out between my legs'

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to 720 Magnolia Way for a 28-year-old female in active labor. Caller states the baby is coming and the mother feels a loop of rope coming out.
clues: Definition & Mechanism: The umbilical cord slips ahead of the presenting fetal part and prolapses through the cervix into the vagina; contractions compress the cord against the pelvis, completely cutting off fetal oxygenation
Visual inspection reveals a pulsating, moist loop of umbilical cord protruding from the vaginal opening

CRITICAL EMERGENCY POSITIONING: Place mother immediately in the KNEE-CHEST POSITION (knees to chest, face down, hips elevated in the air) or steep Trendelenburg to use gravity to slide the fetus away from the cervix

MANDATORY NREMT LIFESAVING PROCEDURE: Insert two sterile gloved fingers into the vagina and gently push the presenting fetal head UPWARD and away from the umbilical cord; MAINTAIN THIS MANUAL DISPLACEMENT CONTINUOUSLY UNTIL SURGICAL CESAREAN SECTION IN THE OR!
ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION: DO NOT attempt to push the cord back inside the vagina! Wrap the exposed cord in sterile gauze moistened with warm sterile saline to prevent vasospasm

baseline_vitals.hr: 104 bpm (tachycardia from labor pain and anxiety)
baseline_vitals.fetal_heart_rate: Cord pulsation felt at 88 bpm (fetal bradycardia indicating active cord compression!)

reassessment_vitals.fetal_heart_rate: Cord pulsations strengthen to 130 bpm (compression successfully relieved!)
reassessment_vitals.pain_score: Contractions continue; fetal head held elevated

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 response to 720 Magnolia Way, 28-year-old female in active labor, cord protruding.
Dispatched to imminent delivery with umbilical cord prolapse. BSI: sterile gloves, mask, eye protection, OB gown. Is the scene safe?
Scene is safe. Father is frantic in the hallway.
Nature of illness: obstetric catastrophe / prolapsed umbilical cord. Two patients (mother and fetus). Requesting ALS backup immediately.
General impression: 28-year-old female on bed, in active labor, clutching her abdomen, screaming: 'My water broke and I feel something hanging out between my legs!'
Hello Maria, I'm EMT Luke. I need to inspect your vaginal opening immediately to protect your baby. Do you consent?
VISUAL INSPECTION: I drape the patient and inspect the perineum. Evaluator, what do I see?
You observe a 4-inch loop of purple umbilical cord protruding from the vaginal opening. Faint pulsations are palpable in the cord at roughly 88 bpm. The fetal head is pressing hard against it.

CRITICAL NREMT LIFESAVING SEQUENCE: STEP 1: POSITIONING. Partner, immediately help Maria into the KNEE-CHEST POSITION (knees drawn to chest, face down, buttocks elevated in the air). Gravity pulls the fetus back into the uterus.

STEP 2: MANUAL FETAL ELEVATION. I don sterile gloves. I gently insert my index and middle fingers into the vagina past the cord, locate the presenting fetal head, and gently push the fetal head UPWARD away from the cord and pelvis. I verbalize: I WILL MAINTAIN MY HAND IN THIS POSITION AND KEEP PRESSURE OFF THE CORD UNTIL AN OB SURGEON TAKES OVER IN THE OR!
As you lift the fetal head upward, the cord pulsations visibly strengthen and accelerate from 88 bpm to 130 bpm.

STEP 3: CORD PROTECTION. Partner, take sterile gauze pads, saturate them with warm sterile normal saline, and wrap them loosely around the exposed umbilical cord. DO NOT ATTEMPT TO PUSH THE CORD BACK INSIDE THE VAGINA. Keep it warm and moist to prevent arterial vasospasm.

STEP 4: OXYGENATION & COACHING. Apply high-flow oxygen via Non-Rebreather mask at 15 L/min to Maria to maximize fetal blood oxygenation. Instruct Maria: 'Maria, do NOT push! Pant through the contractions like blowing out birthday candles!'
Mother's vitals: BP 128/82 mmHg, HR 104, RR 24, SpO2 98% on NRB. Exposed cord remains wrapped and pulsating strongly.

IMMEDIATE CODE 3 EMERGENCY TRANSPORT. We transfer Maria to the stretcher maintaining the knee-chest or steep Trendelenburg position. My gloved hand remains inside the vagina maintaining continuous cephalic displacement throughout extrication and transport.

Contacting Medical Control / Labor & Delivery: 'Labor & Delivery, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. Priority 1 obstetric life-threat arriving in 6 minutes: 28-year-old G3P2 at 39 weeks with an active Prolapsed Umbilical Cord. Mother is in knee-chest position with 15L NRB. Hand is inserted into vagina actively elevating the fetal head off the cord. Fetal pulsations palpable and strong. Cord wrapped in warm sterile saline dressing. Requesting immediate direct transfer onto the Emergency Cesarean Section operating table upon arrival.'
Medic 4, copy! OR 3 is prepped for immediate crash C-section. Bring patient directly through ED doors to the OR suite.
Contractions continue every 2 minutes. Mother is panting. Manual elevation of fetal head is maintained. Cord pulse remains strong at 128 bpm.

On scene, a 4-inch loop of cord was protruding with fetal bradycardia (88 bpm). Immediate knee-chest positioning was instituted, and two sterile gloved fingers were inserted into the vagina to elevate the presenting head off the cord. Cord pulsations accelerated to 130 bpm. Exposed cord wrapped in sterile saline dressing; mother coached not to push and placed on 15L NRB. Fetal head remains manually displaced off the cord right now. Implemented knee-chest positioning, inserted sterile gloved fingers to manually elevate fetal head off the cord, and wrapped exposed loop in warm sterile saline gauze (never pushed back inside). Fetal cord pulsations restored to 130 bpm. Hand maintained in vagina elevating head continuously into the OR for crash C-section.
critical_traps: Attempting to push the prolapsed umbilical cord back inside the vagina (causes severe arterial spasm and fetal demise).
Failing to manually elevate the fetal presenting part off the cord (the fetus will suffocate from cord compression within minutes).
Allowing the mother to push or bear down during contractions (forces the head tighter against the cord).
Allowing the exposed cord to dry out or become cold (causes fatal umbilical artery constriction).
Removing your gloved hand from the vagina before the obstetric surgeon is scrubbed and ready to take over in the OR.

differential_matrix.impact: Prepare for breech delivery; create 'V' airway with fingers if head is trapped.

title: Third-Trimester Bleeding: Placenta Previa vs. Abruptio Placentae

patient.name: Sarah Jenkins
patient.setting: Driver's seat of sedan at traffic intersection
patient.complaint: Sudden severe tearing uterine pain following sudden braking in traffic, dark bleeding

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to intersection of 8th and Elm for a 32-year-old pregnant female involved in a low-speed fender-bender. Caller states patient has severe abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding.
clues: The Critical Diagnostic Differentiation Matrix: 1. ABRUPTIO PLACENTAE: Premature detachment of placenta from uterine wall; characterized by EXCRUCIATING, TEARING, CONSTANT ABDOMINAL PAIN, DARK VENOUS BLEEDING, and a ROCK-HARD, RIGID, HYPERTONIC UTERUS; 2. PLACENTA PREVIA: Placenta abnormally implants over the cervical os; characterized by PAINLESS, BRIGHT RED VAGINAL BLEEDING, and a SOFT, NON-TENDER RELAXED UTERUS
Trauma Mechanism: Sudden deceleration forces (seatbelt compression) shearing the rigid placenta off the elastic uterine wall
Maternal-fetal hemodynamic shock: Maternal hypotension (BP 90/58 mmHg), marked tachycardia (HR 126 bpm), fetal distress
CRITICAL EXAM CONTRAINDICATION: NEVER PERFORM AN INTERNAL DIGITAL VAGINAL EXAMINATION! Direct insertion of fingers can puncture placenta previa or worsen placental separation!

SUPINE HYPOTENSIVE SYNDROME PREVENTION: Transport in the LEFT LATERAL RECUMBENT POSITION (or place a wedge under the right hip to tilt pelvis 15-30 degrees) to prevent the heavy gravid uterus from compressing the Inferior Vena Cava (IVC)

baseline_vitals.lung_sounds: Clear bilaterally

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 response to 8th and Elm, 32-year-old female, 34 weeks pregnant, MVC with severe abdominal pain and bleeding.
Dispatched to pregnant female in MVC with bleeding. BSI: gloves, eye protection, OB gown. Scene safe?
Scene is safe. Fire department has stabilized two vehicles. Low-speed rear-end collision with minor bumper damage. Airbags did not deploy.
Nature of illness: obstetric trauma / third-trimester hemorrhage. Two patients (mother and unborn fetus). Requesting ALS backup immediately.

General impression: 32-year-old visibly pregnant female seated on curb, clutching her heavy gravid abdomen, crying out in severe pain, pale and diaphoretic. Lap seatbelt was worn across lower abdomen. C-spine stabilized.
Hello Sarah, I'm EMT Luke. Are you hurt anywhere besides your stomach?
My neck is fine... but my stomach! Oh God, it feels like my uterus is tearing apart! It's rock hard and won't relax!
Airway is patent. Respirations are 24 breaths/min, rapid. SpO2 is 95%. I apply high-flow oxygen via Non-Rebreather at 15 L/min to maximize fetal placental oxygenation.
Circulation: radial pulse is 126 bpm, rapid and thready. Skin is cool, pale, diaphoretic. BP is 90/58 mmHg. Cap refill is 3 seconds. Priority load-and-go.
OBSTETRIC ABDOMINAL EXAMINATION: I gently palpate Sarah's gravid uterus. What do I feel?
The uterus is rock-hard, rigid, and intensely tender to touch. It does not soften between contractions (uterine tetany / hypertonicity).
I inspect the perineum externally for hemorrhage: What do I see?
You observe dark, venous blood actively dripping from the vaginal opening, soaking her pants. You see no presenting fetal parts.

CRITICAL CLINICAL MANDATE: NO INTERNAL VAGINAL EXAM. I WILL NEVER INSERT FINGERS OR INSTRUMENTS INTO THE VAGINA OF A BLEEDING THIRD-TRIMESTER PATIENT. Doing so could tear a placenta previa or exacerbate placental detachment.

CRITICAL DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS: This is ABRUPTIO PLACENTAE triggered by deceleration seatbelt forces. Hallmarks: 1. Constant tearing uterine pain; 2. Dark venous blood; 3. Rock-hard, rigid, hypertonic uterus. In contrast, Placenta Previa presents with completely painless bright red bleeding and a soft relaxed uterus.

SUPINE HYPOTENSIVE SYNDROME PROTOCOL: We transfer Sarah to the stretcher. If Sarah lies flat on her back, the heavy 34-week uterus compresses the Inferior Vena Cava against her spine, obstructing venous return and worsening shock. I position Sarah in the LEFT LATERAL RECUMBENT POSITION (or place a blanket roll under her right hip to tilt her pelvis 20 to 30 degrees to the left).
Vitals: BP was 90/58, but upon tilting 30 degrees to the left, BP improves to 98/64 mmHg. HR is 114 bpm, RR 20, SpO2 99% on 15L NRB.
I place sanitary pads loosely over the perineum to collect blood and monitor rate of blood loss. Thermal conservation applied.

Contacting Medical Control / OB Trauma: 'Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. Priority 1 emergent transport with a 32-year-old female, 34 weeks gestation, with severe traumatic Abruptio Placentae following an MVC. Presenting with constant tearing uterine agony, rock-hard tetanic uterus, dark vaginal bleeding, and maternal shock (BP 90/58 improving to 98/64 on left lateral tilt, HR 114, 15L NRB). Strictly no internal exam performed. Requesting immediate trauma and high-risk OB surgical activation for emergency Cesarean section at Regional Perinatal Center.'
Medic 4, copy. High-risk OB surgical suite and neonatal resuscitation teams are mobilized.
Uterus remains rigid and tender. Vaginal bleeding continues. BP 98/64, HR 114, RR 20, SpO2 99%.

Perinatal Trauma Surgical Hand-Off Report: 'This is Sarah Jenkins, 32F, 34 weeks gestation, presenting with severe traumatic Abruptio Placentae following deceleration seatbelt trauma. Hallmark presentation: constant excruciating uterine pain, dark venous bleeding, and a rock-hard, rigid, hypertonic uterus. Baseline vitals: BP 90/58, HR 126, RR 24, SpO2 95%. External perineal pads applied without internal examination; placed in left lateral tilt to relieve IVC compression, restoring BP to 98/64, HR 114. 15L NRB applied. Patient is prepped for immediate emergent ultrasound, fetal heart monitoring, and crash Cesarean delivery.'
Masterful differentiation of third-trimester bleeding. Station passed.
hand_off_report: Sarah Jenkins, 32F, 34 weeks gestation, acute traumatic Abruptio Placentae following minor MVC. Classic presentation: constant tearing abdominal pain, dark venous bleeding, and a rigid rock-hard hypertonic uterus. Baseline BP 90/58, HR 126, RR 24. No internal exams performed. Placed on 15L NRB, positioned in left lateral tilt to prevent supine hypotensive IVC compression, improving BP to 98/64, HR 114. Immediate hand-off to high-risk OB surgical team.
critical_traps: Performing an internal digital vaginal examination on a bleeding pregnant patient (lethal risk of tearing placenta previa or worsening detachment).
Transporting a late-term pregnant patient completely flat on her back (causes Supine Hypotensive Syndrome by crushing the IVC, crashing maternal blood pressure and fetal perfusion).
Confusing Abruptio Placentae (painful, dark blood, rigid uterus) with Placenta Previa (painless, bright red blood, soft uterus).
Delaying transport to search for fetal heart tones (fetal survival depends entirely on rapid hospital delivery).
Packing the vagina with gauze or towels (causes severe infection and conceals massive blood pooling).

differential_matrix.clue: PAINLESS, bright red vaginal bleeding, soft non-tender relaxed uterus, no trauma
differential_matrix.impact: Placenta covers cervical os; requires scheduled or emergent C-section; strictly NO internal exam.

title: Neonatal Resuscitation of a Meconium-Depressed Newborn

patient.name: Infant Boy Miller
patient.setting: Living room hardwood floor following precipitous delivery
patient.complaint: Born limp, apneic, cyanotic, covered in thick pea-soup meconium

dispatch: Medic 4, respond priority 1 lights and sirens to 1422 Elmwood Street for a baby born at home. Father states baby is blue, completely limp, and not breathing.
clues: Precipitous home delivery with thick 'pea-soup' meconium-stained amniotic fluid
Depressed Newborn Presentation: Limp muscular tone, cyanotic trunk and extremities, APNEIC (no spontaneous cry or respirations)

THE NEONATAL RESUSCITATION PROGRAM (NRP) GOLDEN MINUTE: 1. Warm, dry, stimulate, position head in 'sniffing position' (do NOT hyperextend!), clear airway with bulb syringe (mouth then nose); 2. Reassess: If still apneic or HR < 100 bpm -> INITIATE POSITIVE PRESSURE VENTILATION (PPV) via neonatal BVM with room air (21% O2) at 40 to 60 breaths/min for 30 seconds

THE RULE OF 60 (CHEST COMPRESSIONS): If heart rate remains LESS THAN 60 BEATS PER MINUTE despite 30 seconds of effective PPV -> BEGIN CHEST COMPRESSIONS IMMEDIATELY at a 3:1 COMPRESSION-TO-VENTILATION RATIO (90 compressions and 30 breaths = 120 events/min) using the two-thumb encircling-hands technique, and increase O2 to 100%
APGAR Scoring: 1-minute APGAR is 1 (Pulse 1, Respiration 0, Tone 0, Reflex 0, Color 0)

reassessment_vitals.hr: 128 bpm (rapid recovery following effective PPV and 3:1 compressions)
reassessment_vitals.rr: 44 breaths/min (vigorous spontaneous respirations, loud lusty cry!)
reassessment_vitals.spo2: 88% at 5 minutes (normal physiologic target for 5-minute newborn)
reassessment_vitals.color: Pink trunk, mild acrocyanosis (pink body, blue hands/feet)

dialogue: Medic 4, priority 1 response to 1422 Elmwood Street, baby born at home, limp and not breathing.
Dispatched to newborn resuscitation. BSI: sterile gloves, mask, eye protection, OB gown. Where is the baby?
Father leads you to the living room. Full-term baby was born 60 seconds ago on a towel. Umbilical cord is intact. Mother is exhausted.
Nature of illness: neonatal cardiopulmonary arrest / depressed meconium newborn. Two patients. Requesting ALS backup immediately.

RAPID INITIAL NEONATAL ASSESSMENT: 1. Is the baby term? Yes. 2. Is the baby breathing or crying? No, completely apneic. 3. Does the baby have good muscle tone? No, completely limp and flaccid. Thick pea-soup meconium is smeared across face.

THE GOLDEN MINUTE - STEP 1: INITIAL CARE (0-30 SECONDS). I immediately clamp the umbilical cord at 6 inches and 8 inches from the abdomen and cut between clamps. I transfer the infant to a dry, warm, flat surface.
I position the head in the neutral 'sniffing position' with a small towel roll under the shoulders. I WILL NOT HYPEREXTEND OR HYPERFLEX THE NECK (closes narrow infant airway).
I suction with a bulb syringe: MOUTH FIRST, THEN NOSE ('M before N' prevents aspirating pharyngeal fluid when nares are stimulated). I suction meconium from mouth and nose.
I vigorously dry the infant with warm towels, discard the wet towels, wrap in dry warm blankets, and flick the soles of the feet to stimulate breathing.
After drying, suctioning, and stimulation, the baby remains limp, completely apneic, and deeply cyanotic. Heart rate auscultated via precordium is 50 beats per minute.

STEP 2: POSITIVE PRESSURE VENTILATION (30-60 SECONDS). The baby is apneic with HR < 100 bpm. I immediately initiate Positive Pressure Ventilation (PPV) using a neonatal Bag-Valve-Mask with room air (21% O2). I ventilate at a rate of 40 to 60 breaths per minute: 'Breathe... two... three... Breathe... two... three...'
Chest is rising gently with each squeeze. SpO2 sensor placed on right wrist (pre-ductal). 30 seconds of PPV delivered.
I reassess heart rate by auscultating the apical pulse for 6 seconds and multiplying by 10. Evaluator, what is the heart rate?
You count 5 beats in 6 seconds: Heart rate is 50 beats per minute. Infant remains apneic.
CRITICAL NRP MANDATE: THE RULE OF 60. Heart rate is LESS THAN 60 BPM despite 30 seconds of effective positive pressure ventilations. CHEST COMPRESSIONS ARE INDICATED IMMEDIATELY.

CHEST COMPRESSION PROTOCOL: I utilize the TWO-THUMB ENCIRCLING-HANDS TECHNIQUE on the lower third of the sternum, compressing one-third the AP diameter of the chest (about 1.5 inches). I coordinate with my partner at a 3:1 COMPRESSION-TO-VENTILATION RATIO (3 compressions to 1 ventilation every 2 seconds = 90 compressions and 30 breaths per minute). I increase oxygen concentration to 100% on the BVM.
After 60 seconds of coordinated 3:1 compressions and 100% ventilations, you pause compressions and auscultate the heart rate.

You hear a rapid, strong heartbeat: 13 beats in 6 seconds = Heart rate is 130 beats per minute! The baby takes a sudden deep breath and lets out a loud, vigorous cry! Extremities begin flexing actively.

HR IS > 100 BPM AND CRYING IS PRESENT! DISCONTINUE CHEST COMPRESSIONS! Discontinue PPV. Place the infant on blow-by oxygen as needed. Keep the baby warm, dry, and place skin-to-skin against mother's chest covered with warm dry blankets.

CALCULATE 5-MINUTE APGAR SCORE: Appearance: pink trunk, blue hands/feet (acrocyanosis) = 1; Pulse: 130 bpm (>100) = 2; Grimace: vigorous cry on stimulation = 2; Activity: active flexion = 2; Respiration: 44 breaths/min strong = 2. Total 5-minute APGAR is 9 out of 10!

Contacting Medical Control / Neonatal ICU: 'Medical Control, this is EMT Candidate on Medic 4. Emergent transport with full-term newborn boy following precipitous home delivery with thick meconium. Initial 1-minute APGAR 1 (apneic, limp, HR 50). Successfully resuscitated per NRP guidelines: warm, dry, sniffing position, suctioned mouth then nose, 30 seconds PPV, followed by 60 seconds of 3:1 compressions and ventilations with 100% O2. Return of Spontaneous Circulation: Current HR 130, spontaneous vigorous cry, 5-minute APGAR 9. Baby is warm and skin-to-skin with mother. Requesting NICU team alert for meconium aspiration monitoring at Regional Children's Hospital.'
Medic 4, magnificent neonatal resuscitation. Children's Hospital NICU team is standing by.

Neonatal Intensive Care Hand-Off Report: 'This is Infant Boy Miller, 10 minutes old, full term, delivered precipitously at home into thick meconium. Initial presentation: completely flaccid, apneic, cyanotic, precordial HR 50 bpm (1-min APGAR 1). Managed via NRP: cleared airway with bulb syringe mouth then nose, dried and stimulated, PPV initiated at 40-60/min for 30s. Heart rate remained 50 bpm, so coordinated 3:1 compressions and 100% ventilations initiated using two-thumb encircling technique for 60s. ROSC achieved: spontaneous cry, HR 130, RR 44, 5-min APGAR 9. Maintained normothermic on mother's chest. Prepped for NICU observation and blood gas evaluation.'
Flawless neonatal resuscitation. Full score awarded. Station passed.
hand_off_report: Infant Boy Miller, full-term newborn, precipitous delivery with thick meconium. Presented limp, apneic, cyanotic, HR 50 bpm (1-min APGAR 1). Executed NRP protocol: suctioned mouth then nose, dried/warmed, 30s PPV at 40-60/min. Due to persistent HR < 60 bpm, executed 3:1 chest compressions with 100% O2 using two-thumb technique for 60s. Full ROSC achieved: vigorous crying, HR 130, RR 44, 5-min APGAR 9. Maintained warm skin-to-skin for NICU transfer.
critical_traps: Failing to initiate positive pressure ventilations when newborn is apneic or HR < 100 bpm after 30 seconds of drying/stimulating.
Failing to initiate chest compressions when heart rate remains < 60 bpm despite 30 seconds of effective PPV (The Rule of 60).
Suctioning the nose before the mouth ('M before N' rule; suctioning nose first triggers gasping and aspiration of pharyngeal meconium).
Hyperextending the newborn's neck (causes immediate airway obstruction; must maintain neutral 'sniffing position').
Allowing the newborn to become hypothermic (cold stress triggers pulmonary hypertension, acidosis, and secondary arrest).
Using a 15:2 or 30:2 compression-ventilation ratio (neonatal CPR requires a strict 3:1 ratio: 90 compressions to 30 breaths per minute!).

differential_matrix.clue: Baby cries vigorously at birth, pink, HR > 120, but exhibits mild grunting or tachypnea (RR 60-80)
differential_matrix.impact: Delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid; supportive blow-by O2; no compressions needed.

differential_matrix.clue: Pink body/mucous membranes with blue hands and feet, vigorous crying, HR > 100
differential_matrix.impact: Completely normal benign finding in first 24 hours of life; score 1 on APGAR color.

differential_matrix.clue: Scaphoid (sunken) abdomen, severe respiratory distress, bowel sounds heard in the left chest
differential_matrix.impact: Avoid positive pressure face mask BVM if possible (distends intestines in chest); requires immediate endotracheal intubation.
